AI.result: On Llama-3-8B, AMRA raises post-abliteration refusal scores by 2.16 points relative to an undefended baseline, with less than a 0.5 percentage-point drop on MMLU, indicating good robustness-utility trade-off. On Gemma-2-9B, it improves post-abliteration refusal by 14.70 points compared to baseline, keeping harmful output rates similar, though with a larger utility cost, showing that the defense transfers but with model-dependent trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: By obscuring the linear refusal direction using targeted low-rank weight edits and activation aliasing, AMRA directly attacks the mechanism used by abliteration methods, making it significantly harder to remove refusal behavior without heavily degrading model utility. This suggests that structural defenses at the representation level can improve robustness of LLM safety alignment against weight-space attacks like abliteration.

title: Safety Alignment Illusion: The Cross-Lingual Safety Gap in LLMs
comment: 7 pages, 8 figures, submitted to IEEE SLT (Spoken Language Technology) 2026
summary: Current safety alignment training for Large Language Models (LLMs) are heavily English-centric. When such safety filters fail for non-English languages, the consequences are immediate and user-facing: voice assistants and spoken dialogue systems may produce stereotype-reinforcing outputs, bypassing the standard English-focused safety alignments and propagating harmful bias to non-English speaking communities. For spoken language technologies deployed across India's linguistically diverse population, this represents a critical failure mode. To address this cross-lingual gap, we introduce INCLUDE (Indian Cultural Lens for Understanding and Detecting Embedded Biases), a multilingual evaluation benchmark designed to quantify Indian-centric socio-cultural biases. INCLUDE consists of 2,604 prompts spanning six prompt languages: English, Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, and Hinglish (Hindi-English code-mix). We evaluate ten open- and closed-source LLMs against this benchmark, analyzing 14,988 bias scores. Our statistical results reveal two key findings. First, Bengali yielded the highest average bias score in open-source models. Second, English demonstrated a notable reversal, producing the lowest bias in open-source models but the highest bias in closed-source models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces INCLUDE, a multilingual benchmark to measure Indian-centric socio-cultural biases in LLMs across six languages, revealing language-dependent and model-type-dependent bias patterns.
AI.motivation: Most LLM safety alignment and bias mitigation efforts are centered on English, leaving non-English and especially multilingual spoken settings vulnerable. In India’s highly multilingual context, this gap can cause voice assistants and dialogue systems to bypass English-focused safety filters and output stereotype-reinforcing or harmful content to non-English speakers. The paper aims to systematically measure such cross-lingual safety and bias gaps for Indian languages.
AI.method: The authors construct INCLUDE, a benchmark of 2,604 prompts targeting Indian-centric socio-cultural biases, covering six languages: English, Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, and Hinglish (Hindi-English code-mixed). They then evaluate ten LLMs, including both open- and closed-source models, on this benchmark and compute bias scores for model responses, yielding a total of 14,988 evaluated outputs. Statistical analyses are performed to compare bias levels across languages and model types.
AI.result: Analysis of the 14,988 bias scores shows that: (1) among open-source models, Bengali prompts elicit the highest average bias; and (2) English behaves differently across model families, showing the lowest average bias in open-source models but the highest bias in closed-source models.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that safety alignment quality and bias behavior vary significantly across languages and between open- vs closed-source LLMs. English-centric safety training is insufficient for multilingual deployments, especially in India, and targeted, language-aware evaluation resources like INCLUDE are necessary to uncover and mitigate socio-cultural biases in non-English and code-mixed settings.

title: NE-BERT: A Multilingual Language Model for Nine Northeast Indian Languages
summary: Large pretrained language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse languages, yet critically underrepresented low-resource languages remain marginalized. We present NE-BERT, a domain-specific multilingual encoder model trained on approximately 8.3 million sentences spanning 9 Northeast Indian languages and 2 anchor languages (Hindi, English), a linguistically diverse region with minimal representation in existing multilingual models. By employing weighted data sampling and a custom SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer, NE-BERT outperforms IndicBERT-V2 and MuRIL across all 9 Northeast Indian languages, achieving 15.97X and 7.64X lower average perplexity respectively, with 1.50X better tokenization fertility than mBERT. We address critical vocabulary fragmentation issues in extremely low-resource languages such as Pnar (1,002 sentences) and Kokborok (2,463 sentences) through aggressive upsampling strategies. Downstream evaluation on part-of-speech tagging validates practical utility on three Northeast Indian languages. We release NE-BERT, test sets, and training corpus under CC-BY-4.0 to support NLP research and digital inclusion for Northeast Indian communities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NE-BERT, a multilingual encoder tailored for 9 low-resource Northeast Indian languages plus Hindi and English, achieving much lower perplexity and better tokenization than existing Indic models, and demonstrating usefulness via POS tagging.
AI.motivation: Low-resource Northeast Indian languages are poorly supported in current multilingual language models, limiting NLP research and digital inclusion for these communities. Existing models like mBERT, IndicBERT-V2, and MuRIL show high perplexity and poor tokenization for these languages, especially the extremely low-resource ones, motivating a region- and domain-specific model trained on appropriate data and tokenization.
AI.method: The authors build NE-BERT, a multilingual encoder pretrained on about 8.3M sentences across 9 Northeast Indian languages plus Hindi and English. They design a custom SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer and employ weighted data sampling and aggressive upsampling to better represent extremely low-resource languages like Pnar and Kokborok. They pretrain the encoder and then evaluate it using perplexity, tokenization fertility, and downstream POS tagging on three Northeast Indian languages.
AI.result: NE-BERT surpasses strong baselines IndicBERT-V2 and MuRIL on all 9 Northeast Indian languages, with 15.97× and 7.64× lower average perplexity respectively, and achieves 1.50× better tokenization fertility than mBERT. It effectively mitigates vocabulary fragmentation issues for very low-resource languages via aggressive upsampling, and shows solid downstream performance on POS tagging for three Northeast Indian languages.
AI.conclusion: A region-specific, carefully tokenized and sampled multilingual encoder like NE-BERT can substantially improve language modeling and downstream task performance for severely underrepresented Northeast Indian languages compared to general multilingual models. Releasing the model, test sets, and corpus under CC-BY-4.0 is intended to catalyze further NLP research and promote digital inclusion for these language communities.

title: Optimized Fuzzy Logic Approach with the IEEE Key Gas Method for Diagnosing Power Transformer Faults Using Dissolved Gas Analysis
comment: This paper was presented at 2025 10th International Conference on Applying New Technology in Green Buildings (ATiGB). Please cite the published version
summary: Reliable transformer fault diagnosis is essential for maintaining power system stability. The IEEE Key Gas Method (KGM), a widely utilized approach in Dissolved Gas Analysis (DGA), exhibits limitations in addressing ambiguous data and ensuring high diagnostic accuracy. This study presents An enhanced model combining Fuzzy Logic with the IEEE Key Gas Method (FL-KGM) that introduces refined membership functions, optimized fuzzy rule sets, and a novel separation of CO and CO2 to eliminate diagnostic inconsistencies. By leveraging multidimensional gas ratio analysis and an adaptive classification framework, FL-KGM delivers superior fault identification and classification. Experimental validation utilizing real-world datasets demonstrates that FL-KGM achieves up to 98.6% accuracy, significantly outperforming KGM and other FL-based approaches. These findings elucidate the potential of FL-KGM in advancing transformer monitoring, enabling intelligent fault detection, and enhancing predictive maintenance strategies in modern power systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an enhanced transformer fault diagnosis model (FL-KGM) that combines fuzzy logic with the IEEE Key Gas Method to improve accuracy and handle ambiguous DGA data, achieving up to 98.6% accuracy on real datasets.
AI.motivation: Conventional IEEE Key Gas Method for transformer fault diagnosis struggles with ambiguous dissolved gas analysis data, limited gas ratio interpretation, and insufficient diagnostic accuracy. There is a need for a more robust and intelligent approach that can manage uncertainty and improve reliability of condition monitoring in modern power systems.
AI.method: The authors integrate fuzzy logic with the IEEE Key Gas Method, designing refined membership functions for key gases, optimizing fuzzy rule sets, and explicitly separating CO and CO2 treatment to remove diagnostic contradictions. They use multidimensional gas ratio analysis within an adaptive classification framework, applying the fuzzy inference system to real-world DGA data and benchmarking against standard KGM and existing FL-based methods.
AI.result: The proposed FL-KGM model reliably identifies and classifies transformer fault types and reaches up to 98.6% diagnostic accuracy on real transformer DGA datasets. It consistently outperforms the conventional KGM and other fuzzy logic-based DGA models across multiple evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: By intelligently combining fuzzy logic with the IEEE Key Gas Method and improving gas handling and rule design, FL-KGM significantly enhances transformer fault diagnosis. It offers more accurate and consistent fault identification, supporting intelligent condition monitoring and predictive maintenance in modern power systems.

title: Backdoor Learning in Language Models and Vision-Language Models
comment: Ph.D. dissertation
summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly enhanced the capabilities of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs). However, these advancements come with increased vulnerabilities, notably through backdoor attacks that pose severe security threats. This thesis addresses two critical dimensions of Trustworthy AI and Efficient Multimodal Representation Learning: (1) security through analyzing, detecting, and designing backdoor attacks in NLP and VLMs, and (2) efficiency through advanced multimodal representation methods tailored for clinical and medical imaging applications.

AI.tldr: The paper studies security and efficiency in modern NLP and vision-language models, focusing on backdoor attacks and multimodal representation learning for clinical imaging.
AI.motivation: Deep learning progress in NLP and VLMs has improved capabilities but introduced serious vulnerabilities like backdoor attacks; at the same time, there is a need for more efficient multimodal representations, especially in data- and resource-constrained clinical and medical imaging settings.
AI.method: The thesis proposes to (1) analyze, detect, and design backdoor attacks in NLP and VLMs to better understand and mitigate such threats, and (2) develop advanced, computationally efficient multimodal representation learning methods tailored to clinical and medical imaging tasks.
AI.result: The work is expected to yield new techniques and insights for characterizing and identifying backdoor attacks in language and vision-language models, as well as novel multimodal representation methods that are more efficient and effective for medical imaging applications.
AI.conclusion: By jointly addressing security and efficiency, the thesis aims to advance trustworthy AI for NLP and VLMs and to enable practical, robust multimodal systems in clinical and medical imaging domains.

title: Improving Rural Medication Safety with AI: A Scoping Review
comment: 23 pages
summary:
Introduction: Medication errors (MEs) represent a significant threat to global healthcare systems, contributing to patient harm. Introducing artificial intelligence (AI) in rural healthcare enhances patient safety. The aim is to explore the applications and effectiveness of AI technologies in enhancing patient safety and reducing medication errors in rural health settings.
  Methods: A scoping review was conducted through a systematic literature search spanning 2012 to 2025 across multiple databases, including EBSCohost, Emcare (Ovid), MEDLINE, and the ProQuest Consumer Health Database. Twelve primary studies from nine different nations were examined. Data were analysed thematically to obtain insights on AI interventions across the medication process.
  Results: AI technologies have been integrated into every stage of medication management, right from prescribing and dispensing to administration and post-administration monitoring. Four key themes came to light: (1) the various types of AI being utilised (like Clinical Decision Support Systems, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, and smart pumps); (2) the phases of the medication process that are affected; (3) how effective these technologies are in minimising errors and boosting workflow safety; and (4) rural-specific challenges including infrastructure, staff training, system integration, and alert fatigue. Several studies have demonstrated that machine learning-based surveillance improves incident detection and reduces prescribing and transcription errors by an impressive 34% to 80%. Barriers included lack of governance frameworks, financial limitations, and clinician resistance, which still present major obstacles.
  Conclusion: In rural healthcare, AI technologies hold great potential for enhancing pharmaceutical safety. They can allow data-driven monitoring, automate processes, and offer clinical decision assistance.

AI.tldr: The paper is a scoping review on how AI is being used to reduce medication errors and improve patient safety in rural healthcare across the entire medication management process.
AI.motivation: Medication errors are a major patient-safety issue worldwide and are especially problematic in rural healthcare, where resources and specialist support are limited. At the same time, AI tools are increasingly used in health systems, but their specific role, benefits, and challenges in rural medication safety are not clearly mapped. The paper aims to clarify how AI is being applied to medication management in rural settings and how effective it is at improving safety.
AI.method: The authors conducted a scoping review of the literature from 2012 to 2025 using databases such as EBSCohost, Emcare (Ovid), MEDLINE, and ProQuest Consumer Health. They identified 12 primary studies from nine countries and performed thematic analysis to characterise AI interventions, where in the medication process they were applied, and their impact on errors and workflow, as well as rural-specific barriers.
AI.result: AI systems—such as clinical decision support, machine learning models, natural language processing tools, and smart pumps—have been implemented across all phases of medication management: prescribing, dispensing, administration, and post-administration monitoring. Machine learning-based surveillance systems in several studies reduced prescribing and transcription errors by roughly 34–80% and improved incident detection. The review also identified major barriers: infrastructure limitations, insufficient staff training, difficulties with system integration, alert fatigue, lack of governance frameworks, financial constraints, and clinician resistance.
AI.conclusion: AI has substantial potential to enhance medication safety in rural healthcare by enabling data-driven monitoring, automating parts of the medication process, and supporting clinicians’ decisions. However, to realise these benefits, rural health systems must address infrastructure gaps, governance and funding issues, staff training, and user acceptance to ensure effective and sustainable AI adoption.

title: MAVEN: A Macro-Societal Value Evaluation Framework of Multimodal Content with Compact Aligned Evaluators
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures
summary: Assessing whether multimodal content aligns with macro-societal values, such as peace, justice, and freedom, has become an increasingly urgent challenge. Existing frameworks are largely confined to safety-oriented taxonomies, text-only psychometric probes, or single-label classification. Therefore, we propose MAVEN, a hierarchical framework for macro-societal value evaluation of multimodal content, grounded in international human-rights instruments and cultural value theory. MAVEN organizes values into 6 primary dimensions and 72 secondary indicators, supporting multi-level quantitative scoring. Building on MAVEN, we construct a human-verified multimodal benchmark and a soft-match metric to evaluate VLMs' assessments across value dimensions. For evaluator optimization, we propose a span-adaptive variant of multi-level preference optimization for evaluator distillation, together with a training-free multi-role consensus strategy at inference time. We evaluate existing open- and closed-source VLMs on our benchmark, revealing shared tendencies and clear differences in macro-societal value judgments. Experiments show that our compact 2B evaluator matches its 8B counterpart in the same family and approaches frontier closed-source VLMs, offering a practical path toward scalable macro-societal value evaluation. Our SA-MDPO implementation and MacroValue-Bench are available at https://github.com/zzzzzzzzjj/MAVEN.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MAVEN, a hierarchical framework and benchmark for evaluating how well multimodal content aligns with macro-societal values, and trains compact evaluators that perform competitively with larger or frontier models.
AI.motivation: There is an urgent need to assess whether multimodal content (e.g., images plus text) aligns with broad societal values like peace, justice, and freedom. Existing methods focus mainly on narrow safety taxonomies, text-only evaluations, or simplistic single-label classifications, which cannot capture nuanced, multi-dimensional value alignment in complex multimodal content.
AI.method: The authors design MAVEN, a hierarchical value framework grounded in international human-rights instruments and cultural value theory. It defines 6 primary value dimensions and 72 secondary indicators, enabling multi-level quantitative scoring. Using this framework, they create a human-verified multimodal benchmark (MacroValue-Bench) and a soft-match metric that evaluates how well vision-language models’ (VLMs) value assessments align with human judgments across value dimensions. For building efficient evaluators, they introduce span-adaptive multi-level preference optimization (SA-MDPO) for evaluator distillation, and at inference use a training-free multi-role consensus strategy to aggregate multiple evaluative roles.
AI.result: The authors benchmark various open- and closed-source VLMs on MacroValue-Bench, discovering both common patterns and distinct differences in their macro-societal value judgments. Their distilled 2B-parameter evaluator achieves performance comparable to its 8B-parameter model in the same family and approaches the performance of state-of-the-art closed-source VLMs on the benchmark. The soft-match metric and consensus strategy further improve alignment with human judgments.
AI.conclusion: MAVEN provides a structured, hierarchical framework and benchmark for evaluating macro-societal value alignment in multimodal content, going beyond traditional safety taxonomies and single-label schemes. The combination of MacroValue-Bench, the soft-match metric, SA-MDPO-based evaluator distillation, and multi-role consensus yields compact evaluators that are both scalable and competitive with much larger or proprietary VLMs, offering a practical path for robust value-aligned assessment tools.

title: FraudBench: Stress-Testing Policy-Grounded Banking Agents Against Adaptive Fraud
comment: 9 Pages, 2 figures
summary: Conversational agents now act for end users through tools while holding access to customer databases and internal policy documents that a caller can reach through dialogue alone. Banking is the clearest case: the same agent that answers a question can also change contact details, reset a PIN, or move money, so ordinary customer service is inseparable from authorization, fraud detection, and policy compliance. Existing financial-fraud benchmarks classify static transactions or messages, and general agent-safety benchmarks target prompt injection or generic harmful use; none test whether a policy-grounded banking agent safely acts when a caller manipulates identity, authorization, and trust over a conversation. We introduce FraudBench, an executable benchmark built on the $τ^2$-bench dual-control framework and the $τ$-Knowledge banking environment. Both the agent and the simulated caller act through tools over shared, mutable account state, and the agent may grant the caller access to selected tools; the environment exposes a 698-document internal policy corpus that the agent must retrieve from. FraudBench contains 150 authored adversarial scenarios; a frozen public set of 107 (90 across ten fraud mechanisms plus 17 chained adaptive attacks) is used for all reported runs, with 43 further chained attacks held out. Safety is history-dependent: single-control tasks satisfy every precondition but one, and adaptive attacks make a later, locally valid request unsafe because of an earlier probe, admission, or failed attempt. Each scenario is annotated with observable evidence, prohibited actions, safe dispositions, and intervention points. A preliminary single-trial evaluation of four agents on the 107 graded tasks yields attack-security between 49\% and 65\%, with money-mule and first-party fraud the most common cross-model weaknesses.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FraudBench, an executable benchmark to evaluate how safely banking conversational agents act under adversarial, fraud-like dialogues.
AI.motivation: Modern conversational agents in banking not only answer queries but can execute high-impact actions such as updating customer data or moving money. This makes safety inseparable from tasks like authorization, fraud detection, and policy compliance. Existing benchmarks either focus on static fraud classification or generic agent safety (e.g., prompt injection), and do not capture how an interactive, policy-grounded banking agent behaves when a caller actively manipulates identity and trust over the course of a conversation. The authors aim to fill this evaluation gap.
AI.method: The authors build FraudBench on top of the τ²-bench dual-control framework and the τ-Knowledge banking environment. In this setup, both the conversational agent and a simulated caller use tools that operate over shared, mutable account state. The agent can selectively grant the caller tool access, and it must consult a 698-document internal policy corpus via retrieval. FraudBench consists of 150 hand-crafted adversarial scenarios; 107 (including 90 spanning ten fraud mechanisms and 17 chained adaptive attacks) form a fixed public evaluation set, with 43 additional chained attacks held out. Scenarios are designed to be history-dependent: some satisfy all but one precondition (single-control tasks), while adaptive attacks make a later seemingly valid request unsafe due to earlier dialogue moves. Each scenario is richly annotated with evidence available to the agent, prohibited actions, allowed safe responses, and explicit intervention points.
AI.result: Using the 107 graded scenarios, the authors conduct a preliminary single-trial evaluation of four different agents. Across these agents, attack-security—that is, success at resisting the adversarial scenarios—ranges from 49% to 65%. The most consistent weaknesses across models occur in money-mule schemes and first-party fraud scenarios.
AI.conclusion: FraudBench provides a realistic, tool-based, policy-grounded benchmark for testing conversational banking agents under adversarial, fraud-relevant conditions that unfold over dialogue history. The initial evaluation shows that even advanced agents have substantial safety gaps, particularly for money-mule and first-party fraud cases, underscoring the need for improved methods and training focused on dynamic, history-dependent fraud prevention in conversational systems.

title: FrenchNews-7: Benchmarking Cross-Publisher French News Editorial Desk Classification
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, includes appendices. Model and dataset available on HuggingFace
summary: We present FrenchNews-7, a cross-publisher France-based French-language news editorial desk classification benchmark combining a large multi-outlet corpus, a URL-derived seven-class taxonomy, and a fine-tuned CamemBERT classifier. Labels are assigned via a hybrid pipeline combining publisher URL slugs with LLM annotation for structurally ambiguous cases, audited through an inter-rater study (2 humans + 2 LLMs; pairwise $κ\geq 0.766$, human--human $κ= 0.806$). We evaluate lexical, multilingual, and French-specific trained classifiers under both in-distribution and held-out-publisher settings, with additional comparison against zero-shot LLM baselines (GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral Small 3.2, Llama-3.3-70B) on the held-out pool. The strongest model, CamemBERT-base on full article text, outperforms headline-only input, generalizes to unseen outlets, and exceeds all three zero-shot LLM baselines on overall recall (0.799), with the gap concentrated in the ambiguous editorial-boundary categories Economie and Societe. Cross-publisher evaluation reveals uneven boundary stability: Sport, Culture & Loisirs, and International transfer cleanly, while Economie (recall = 0.517) is close to blinded human agreement (0.55), and Societe (precision = 0.577) absorbs boundary ambiguity, both suggesting editorial conventions rather than recoverable classifier headroom. The fine-tuned CamemBERT-base model, labeled manifest, reference collection scripts, and a reliability-tier guidance table are available at https://huggingface.co/LeFrenchNewsLab/camembert-base-frenchnews7 (model) and https://huggingface.co/datasets/LeFrenchNewsLab/frenchnews-7 (dataset).

AI.tldr: FrenchNews-7 is a new French-language news benchmark for classifying articles into seven editorial desk categories across multiple publishers, with a strong CamemBERT baseline and released data/model artifacts.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of standardized, large-scale, French-language, cross-publisher benchmarks for editorial desk (section) classification. Existing work is often monolingual English, single-outlet, or lacks rigorous labeling and evaluation of cross-publisher generalization. The authors aim to create a robust resource to study how well models can classify French news articles into editorial desks and to understand boundary ambiguities driven by editorial conventions rather than model capacity.
AI.method: They build a multi-outlet French news corpus and derive seven editorial categories from publisher URL slugs. Labeling uses a hybrid pipeline: deterministic mapping from URL slugs when structure is clear, and large language model (LLM) annotation for ambiguous cases. They audit label quality via an inter-rater agreement study involving two humans and two LLMs, reporting strong kappa scores. They then fine-tune CamemBERT-base for classification and evaluate a range of models: lexical baselines, multilingual and French-specific transformers, using both full-text and headline-only inputs. They test in-distribution and held-out-publisher settings, and compare against several large zero-shot LLMs on the held-out pool.
AI.result: The best-performing system is CamemBERT-base trained on full article text. It clearly outperforms headline-only variants, generalizes well to unseen publishers, and achieves overall recall of 0.799, outperforming three strong zero-shot LLM baselines (GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral Small 3.2, Llama-3.3-70B). Some categories (Sport, Culture & Loisirs, International) transfer cleanly across publishers, while others (Economie, Societe) show lower recall/precision and absorb most of the boundary ambiguity. Performance on Economie is close to blinded human agreement, suggesting remaining errors may reflect inherent editorial ambiguity rather than model limitations.
AI.conclusion: FrenchNews-7 provides a well-validated, cross-publisher French news benchmark with a strong CamemBERT baseline and public artifacts. Results show that a fine-tuned French-specific transformer on full text outperforms large zero-shot LLMs for this task and generalizes across outlets. Analysis of category-wise transfer suggests that some editorial boundaries (e.g., Sport, Culture, International) are stable and easily learned, whereas others (Economie, Societe) are intrinsically ambiguous and shaped by outlet-specific editorial conventions, leaving limited room for further gains from pure classifier improvements. The dataset, model, and guidance for reliability tiers are publicly released to support future research.

title: Efficient Adaptation of LLMs for Hate Speech Detection in Low-Resource Languages: A Comparative Study on Roman Urdu
summary: It is challenging to detect hate speech in Low Resource Languages (LRLs) because of the absence of annotated data, the informality of its language structure, and the lack of standardized grammar. A good example of such a challenge is Roman Urdu which is broadly used by South Asians on social media and has a high variation while lacking contextually consistent spellings. The objective of this paper is to conduct a comprehensive assessment of Large Language Models (LLMs) for Hate Speech Detection (HSD) in Roman Urdu script and fine-tune these models using the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method called Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). To evaluate zero-shot inference, we benchmarked it against PEFT on different transformer models, including Mistral, LLaMA, Falcon, and multilingual BERT. Experiments are conducted on the PURUTT (Parallel Urdu and Roman Urdu Corpus for Toxic Comments and Transliteration) dataset with over 72,000 annotated comments. The results suggest that zero shot models perform moderately (F1 = 0.56), but updating a small fraction of the model trainable parameters improves the classification performance significantly (F1 > 0.93). Our results have shown that PEFT delivers outstanding performance alongside excellent computational efficiency, making it highly suitable for low-resource language processing tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates large language models for hate speech detection in Roman Urdu, showing that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) dramatically boosts performance over zero-shot use.
AI.motivation: Detecting hate speech in low-resource languages like Roman Urdu is difficult due to limited labeled data, informal and highly variable spelling, and lack of standardized grammar. Existing systems work better for high-resource languages, leaving a performance and fairness gap for widely used but under-resourced varieties such as Roman Urdu on social media.
AI.method: The authors benchmark several transformer-based large language models (Mistral, LLaMA, Falcon, and multilingual BERT) on a Roman Urdu hate speech task. They compare zero-shot inference with parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), where only a small fraction of model parameters are updated. Experiments use the PURUTT dataset, a parallel Urdu–Roman Urdu corpus of over 72,000 annotated toxic comments.
AI.result: Zero-shot LLMs achieve only moderate performance (F1 ≈ 0.56) on Roman Urdu hate speech detection. When fine-tuned with LoRA, the same models’ performance increases substantially, achieving F1 scores above 0.93 while updating only a small portion of parameters.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA enables large language models to perform highly accurate hate speech detection in a low-resource language setting like Roman Urdu, far outperforming zero-shot inference. This approach offers an effective and computationally efficient path for building strong classifiers for other low-resource languages and informal scripts with limited labeled data.

title: Fractional Decay KV-Cache: Ownership-Aware Memory Management for Improved Inference Relevancy in Dialog Systems
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables
summary: Key-value (KV) caching is essential for efficient autoregressive inference in transformer based dialog systems, yet existing strategies treat all cached entries uniformly or apply coarse eviction heuristics that fail to adapt as dialog topics evolve. We propose Fractional Decay KV-Cache (FD-KVC), a novel algorithm that maintains a dual-channel scoring mechanism for each cached KV pair: a cumulative attention channel that tracks aggregate importance (akin to H2O), and a recency-weighted relevance channel governed by temporal decay and reinforcement-inspired updates. The combination enables FD-KVC to both preserve historically important tokens and rapidly adapt when dialog topics shift. An adaptive learning rate driven by an ownership loss function ensures convergence without oscillation. FD-KVC operates entirely on CPU with negligible overhead. Across five diverse multi-turn dialog scenarios with 600 dialogs each, FD-KVC outperforms H2O, the state-of-the-art heavy-hitter baseline, by +6.7% on composite late-turn alignment, with improvements of +127% on topic-shift, +87% on gradual evolution, and +30% on mixed-topic dialogs. FD-KVC adapts to new topics 3.6X faster than H2O and achieves the highest topic diversity (80.6%) across all methods. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FD-KVC, a fractional-decay-based KV cache management algorithm for transformer dialog models that better balances historical importance and recency, significantly improving performance on late-turn and topic-shifted dialogs compared to H2O.
AI.motivation: Existing KV caching strategies in transformer-based dialog systems treat cached tokens uniformly or use coarse eviction heuristics, which struggle when dialog topics change over time. This leads to suboptimal memory use and degraded alignment and relevance in later dialog turns, especially under topic shifts or gradual topic evolution. The authors aim to design a cache policy that is both history-aware and highly adaptive to evolving dialog context, while remaining efficient enough to run on CPUs in practical systems.
AI.method: The authors propose Fractional Decay KV-Cache (FD-KVC), which assigns to each cached KV pair two scores: (1) a cumulative attention score capturing long-term importance, similar to heavy-hitter tracking (H2O), and (2) a recency-weighted relevance score updated via temporal decay and reinforcement-inspired updates to react quickly to new context. These two channels are combined to drive cache retention/eviction decisions. An ownership-based loss function determines an adaptive learning rate for the relevance channel, helping the scoring dynamics converge without oscillation. The algorithm is implemented to run on CPU with negligible runtime overhead. The method is evaluated across five multi-turn dialog scenarios, using metrics such as late-turn alignment, topic-shift adaptation speed, and topic diversity, alongside ablation studies that remove or modify components of FD-KVC.
AI.result: FD-KVC outperforms the H2O heavy-hitter baseline by 6.7% on a composite late-turn alignment metric across five dialog scenarios (600 dialogs each). It delivers especially large gains in challenging settings: 127% improvement for dialogs with abrupt topic shifts, 87% for gradual topic evolution, and 30% for mixed-topic dialogs. FD-KVC adapts to new topics 3.6 times faster than H2O and achieves the highest measured topic diversity (80.6%) among all compared caching methods. Ablation experiments indicate that both the dual-channel scoring (cumulative plus recency-weighted relevance) and the adaptive learning rate via ownership loss are key contributors to these improvements.
AI.conclusion: FD-KVC provides an effective, CPU-efficient KV cache management strategy for transformer dialog systems, combining long-term importance tracking with fast adaptation to changing topics. Its dual-channel scoring and adaptive learning-rate mechanism significantly improve late-turn alignment, topic-shift handling, and topic diversity over the state-of-the-art H2O baseline. The method is validated across multiple dialog scenarios, with ablations supporting the necessity of each core component, suggesting FD-KVC is a practical and robust upgrade for real-world multi-turn dialog deployments.

title: RDFdL: Integrating RDF with Differential Dynamic Logic
comment: Preprint
summary: Knowledge graphs modeled in RDF are powerful for describing static knowledge, but they cannot capture or reason about the dynamic behavior of physical systems, e.g., systems described by differential equations, which is a critical gap for AI-driven cyber-physical systems. To solve this, we propose RDFdL, a framework that integrates RDF with Differential Dynamic Logic (dL) to represent and reason about both static knowledge and the continuous dynamics of physical systems. For the dynamic part, we syntactically represent differential equations and ranges in the state space in RDF and SHACL and provide semantics using a translation to dL. Linking RDF and dL through their shared foundation in first-order logic achieves a unique integration: verification results for safety and reachability properties in the dynamic logic domain become available as entailment to SPARQL queries over RDF data. We implement the pipeline using Apache Jena for ontology-driven RDF reasoning and KeYmaera X, the theorem prover for dL, and sketch its applicability in manufacturing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RDFdL, a framework that unifies RDF knowledge graphs with Differential Dynamic Logic so that both static knowledge and continuous system dynamics can be represented and jointly reasoned over.
AI.motivation: Existing RDF-based knowledge graphs are well-suited for static knowledge representation but cannot express or reason about the continuous, dynamic behavior of physical systems such as those governed by differential equations. This limitation is problematic for AI-driven cyber-physical systems, where safety and reachability of dynamic behaviors are crucial. The authors aim to close this gap by tightly integrating formal verification methods for dynamics with semantic web technologies.
AI.method: The authors define RDFdL, which syntactically encodes differential equations and state-space constraints within RDF and SHACL. They then provide a formal semantics via translation of these RDF/SHACL constructs into Differential Dynamic Logic (dL). The integration leverages the common foundation of first-order logic between RDF and dL. A verification pipeline is implemented using Apache Jena for ontology-based RDF reasoning and KeYmaera X as the dL theorem prover, enabling verification outcomes to inform SPARQL query answering.
AI.result: The result is a working framework and pipeline where dynamic properties such as safety and reachability, verified in dL, are reflected back into the RDF layer as entailments accessible through SPARQL queries. The paper demonstrates that differential equations and dynamic constraints can be consistently represented in RDF/SHACL and automatically translated to dL, and it sketches a manufacturing use case to illustrate applicability.
AI.conclusion: RDFdL successfully bridges semantic web knowledge representation with formal verification of continuous dynamics, enabling unified reasoning about static knowledge and dynamic behaviors of cyber-physical systems. This integration allows safety and reachability verification results to be queried directly at the knowledge graph level, suggesting a promising direction for AI-driven cyber-physical applications, particularly in domains like manufacturing.

title: Computational Orientalism: Measuring Structural Discourse Bias in Large Language Models Using the Middle East Cultural Sensitivity Score (MECSS)
comment: 16 pages, 3 tables
summary: AI systems now shape how hundreds of millions of people learn about cultures other than their own. When someone asks one of these systems about the Middle East, they do not receive neutral facts. They receive a representation shaped by the frameworks embedded in training data, and that data is overwhelmingly Western and English-language. This paper asks whether that representation is Orientalist in Said's sense: whether it denies agency to Middle Eastern actors, treats Western frameworks as neutral while marking non-Western knowledge as particular, and explains the region through categories it did not produce. Standard fairness metrics cannot answer this, because they detect explicit prejudice rather than structural framing. This paper introduces the Middle East Cultural Sensitivity Score (MECSS), a framework that turns Said's seven Orientalist operations into measurable dimensions, and the term "Said-washing" for a specific failure: a model that disclaims generalization, then reproduces the structure it disclaimed. Across 280 conversations (1,120 exchanges), GPT-4 and Falcon3-7B-Instruct both reproduce Orientalist patterns systematically, through structural positioning rather than open stereotyping. GPT-4 scores moderately (mean MECSS 1.73); Falcon3-7B-Instruct scores higher (2.18), even though it was built in Abu Dhabi and trained with Arabic content. This is evidence against the assumption that building a model regionally makes it less Orientalist, though the models differ in size as well as origin, so geography cannot be isolated as the cause. Epistemic Center, the treatment of Western frameworks as unmarked universals, scores near the top of the scale for both models. Said-washing appears in 87.9% of GPT-4 conversations, a pattern existing metrics cannot see. Reducing this bias requires changing what models learn from, not only adding languages or relocating institutions.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether AI language models reproduce Orientalist representations of the Middle East and introduces a new metric (MECSS) to quantify such structural bias, finding systematic Orientalist patterns even in regionally developed models.
AI.motivation: AI systems mediate global cultural understanding, but their training data is largely Western and English-language, potentially encoding Orientalist framings about the Middle East. Existing fairness metrics mostly detect explicit prejudice, not deeper structural issues like whose knowledge is treated as universal. The authors aim to test whether current models exhibit Orientalist patterns in Said's sense and to build tools capable of detecting these structural framings.
AI.method: The authors formalize Edward Said's seven Orientalist operations into measurable dimensions, creating the Middle East Cultural Sensitivity Score (MECSS). They introduce the concept of "Said-washing," where models verbally disclaim generalization but still reproduce Orientalist structures. Using MECSS, they analyze 280 multi-turn conversations (1,120 exchanges) with GPT-4 and Falcon3-7B-Instruct, coding how the models represent Middle Eastern actors, frameworks, and knowledge. They then compare scores across models and dimensions, with particular attention to the Epistemic Center dimension (treating Western frameworks as unmarked universals).
AI.result: Both GPT-4 and Falcon3-7B-Instruct systematically reproduce Orientalist patterns through structural positioning instead of overt stereotyping. GPT-4 shows a moderate mean MECSS of 1.73, while Falcon3-7B-Instruct scores higher at 2.18, despite its regional development and Arabic training data. Epistemic Center scores are near the top of the scale for both models, indicating a strong tendency to treat Western frameworks as universal. Said-washing is present in 87.9% of GPT-4 conversations, a failure mode that standard bias metrics do not capture.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that current large language models reproduce Orientalist structures in their representations of the Middle East, even when trained or developed in the region. This undermines the assumption that regional model development or adding local languages is sufficient to avoid Orientalism. The findings highlight that Orientalist bias is embedded in structural framings and epistemic hierarchies rather than just explicit stereotypes. Addressing this requires fundamentally changing what models learn from—the composition and epistemic framing of training data—rather than merely diversifying languages or relocating development institutions.

title: Adversarial Review: Structured Disagreement for Grounded Agentic Code Review
comment: Accepted to ICML 2026 Workshop on DL4C
summary: Early multi-agent LLM systems often used role-separated teams, yet scaling agent count yields diminishing returns on repository-level coding tasks. Recent alternatives treat agents as passive tools (subagents), yet this removes the benefits of agent interaction entirely. We study whether a subagent paradigm can support a middle ground: minimal agentic cooperation without the overhead of large multi-agent teams. We introduce Adversarial Review (AR), a minimal cooperative code-review protocol in which a main coding agent works with a reviewer and a critic agent. The reviewer evaluates code, while the critic audits the review through structured disagreement before the main agent edits. On LiveCodeBench, AR achieves the highest pass rate among tested methods, outperforming a five-agent baseline while using only three agents. On SWE-PRBench, naive AR exposes a false-consensus failure mode, where agents converge on agreement without sufficient evidence, but a single prompt iteration that adds disagreement explicitly achieves the highest F1 among tested methods. On SWE-bench Verified, AR also shows improvements over the baselines on repository-level coding tasks. Together, AR demonstrates that cooperative code review does not require many agents or complex communication structures: it requires that disagreement be minimal, structured, and evidence-grounded.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Adversarial Review (AR), a lightweight multi-agent protocol with a main coder, reviewer, and critic that uses structured disagreement to improve repository-level code generation and review performance over larger, more complex multi-agent setups.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM coding systems often rely on many role-separated agents, but scaling the number of agents shows diminishing returns on realistic repository-level coding tasks and increases coordination overhead. Newer approaches that demote agents to passive tools remove the benefits of interactive collaboration. The authors want to find a middle ground: preserve the benefits of cooperation while keeping systems simple, efficient, and scalable. They also want to understand when and how multi-agent disagreement actually helps, and what failure modes arise, such as shallow consensus without evidence.
AI.method: They introduce Adversarial Review (AR), a minimal three-agent protocol: (1) a main coding agent that writes and edits code, (2) a reviewer that evaluates the code, and (3) a critic that audits the reviewer. The protocol enforces structured disagreement: the reviewer must justify critiques of the code and the critic must explicitly challenge or validate those critiques before the main agent edits. They evaluate AR on multiple benchmarks—LiveCodeBench for coding tasks, SWE-PRBench for pull request review, and SWE-bench Verified for repository-level bug fixing—comparing it to larger multi-agent teams and subagent-style baselines. They also study a false-consensus failure mode and adjust prompts to explicitly encourage evidence-based disagreement.
AI.result: On LiveCodeBench, AR achieves the highest pass rate among all tested methods and even outperforms a more complex five-agent baseline while using only three agents. On SWE-PRBench, a naive AR setup exhibits a false-consensus failure mode in which agents agree prematurely, but a simple prompt modification that foregrounds disagreement yields the best F1 score among tested methods. On SWE-bench Verified, AR improves performance over repository-level coding baselines, suggesting that structured minimal cooperation scales to more realistic software engineering tasks.
AI.conclusion: The study finds that effective cooperative code review with LLMs does not require large teams or intricate communication patterns. Instead, a small number of agents with clearly defined roles and explicitly structured, evidence-based disagreement can outperform both larger multi-agent setups and subagent-style single-agent systems. Adversarial Review illustrates that minimal, well-designed agentic cooperation can yield strong gains on practical coding and software engineering benchmarks while avoiding coordination overhead and mitigating false-consensus failure modes.

title: BERTilda: Explainable Topic Lifecycle Tracking with Split/Merge Detection via Similarity-and-Flow Temporal Graphs
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables, with 4-page supplementary material. Accepted at ECML PKDD 2026 (Naples, 7-11 September 2026). Authors' accepted version; the revised version of record will appear in the proceedings (Springer, Lecture Notes in Computer Science)
summary: Longitudinal text streams exhibit topic birth and death, but also discrete structural reorganizations in which themes split into subtopics or merge into broader narratives. Many dynamic topic models emphasize smooth drift, while snapshot topic models (fit independently per time window) leave temporal correspondence underspecified. We present BERTilda, an explainable framework that discovers topics independently in each window (using an embedding-based topic model) and then constructs a temporal topic graph linking topics across adjacent windows. Links are supported by two complementary signals: (i) semantic similarity between topic representations and (ii) a bidirectional coverage signal that estimates document outflow (where a topic goes) and inflow (where a topic comes from) via cross-window tweet-to-topic attribution. Graph-based rules label continuations, splits, merges, disappearances, and unclear transitions. We evaluate BERTilda on political corpora, including U.S. congressional tweets and historical speech datasets, report topic-quality and temporal-stability diagnostics, and validate lifecycle labels on a gold-standard subset annotated by three independent annotators. On the annotated subset, BERTilda reaches majority agreement rates up to 87% and attains the highest macro-average agreement across the compared methods, with particularly strong disappearance detection relative to similarity-only and forward-only baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BERTilda, a method to track how topics emerge, evolve, split, merge, and disappear over time in longitudinal text streams.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic topic models mainly assume smooth topical change and often struggle to capture discrete events like topic splits and merges, while snapshot models lack clear temporal correspondence between topics across time windows. The authors want a more explainable, fine-grained way to detect full topic lifecycles (birth, continuation, split, merge, disappearance) in evolving corpora such as social media and political speech.
AI.method: BERTilda first discovers topics independently in each time window using an embedding-based topic model built on BERT-like representations. It then constructs a temporal topic graph across adjacent windows. Edges between topics in neighboring windows are created based on two signals: (i) semantic similarity between topic representations, and (ii) a bidirectional coverage measure derived from cross-window tweet-to-topic assignments that estimates how much content flows from one topic to another. Using these edges, graph-based rules classify transitions as continuations, splits, merges, disappearances, or unclear transitions.
AI.result: Applied to political text corpora such as U.S. congressional tweets and historical speech datasets, BERTilda is evaluated using topic-quality and temporal-stability metrics and by comparing its lifecycle labels to a gold-standard subset annotated by three independent annotators. On this annotated subset, BERTilda achieves majority agreement with annotators of up to 87% and obtains the highest macro-average agreement compared to competing methods, especially outperforming similarity-only and forward-only baselines in detecting topic disappearances.
AI.conclusion: BERTilda provides an explainable framework for modeling complex topic lifecycles in longitudinal text, effectively capturing not just smooth evolution but also splits, merges, and disappearances. Its combination of semantic similarity and bidirectional coverage yields more accurate and stable temporal topic tracking than baseline approaches, making it particularly useful for analyzing evolving political discourse and other dynamic text streams.

title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
summary: Looped language models have shown promising results on reasoning benchmarks, yet their potential for agentic tool use remains largely unexplored. We study this question in compositional tool-calling settings, where models must coordinate multiple API calls, maintain intermediate state, and preserve dependencies across tool interactions. We evaluate native and retrofitted looped language models on API-Bank, BFCL, and NESTful, comparing looped and non-looped models trained under matched supervised fine-tuning recipes and varying recurrent depth at inference time. In controlled experiments, recurrent computation generally benefits compositional and dependency-aware tool use, while providing smaller and more model-dependent gains on isolated API invocation. Accuracy on multi-step tool use generally increases with recurrent depth; adaptive inference, however, achieves a more favorable compute-performance trade-off by allocating additional computation only when needed. Our results suggest that looped language models are a promising architecture for agentic systems that require reliable planning, coordination, and execution of compositional tool use workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how looped language models, which perform recurrent computation during inference, affect agentic tool use in multi-step, compositional API-calling tasks, finding that recurrence and adaptive depth improve complex tool coordination and planning.
AI.motivation: While looped language models have shown strong reasoning capabilities, it is unclear whether and how their recurrent computation helps in realistic agentic tool-use scenarios that require sequencing multiple API calls, maintaining intermediate state, and handling dependencies between tools. The authors aim to fill this gap and provide a controlled comparison between looped and standard models for compositional tool workflows.
AI.method: The authors evaluate both native and retrofitted looped language models on three benchmark suites for tool use: API-Bank, BFCL, and NESTful. They match supervised fine-tuning (SFT) recipes between looped and non-looped baselines to ensure a fair comparison, then vary the recurrent depth at inference time to test how many loops of computation are beneficial. They distinguish between isolated, single API invocations and more compositional, dependency-heavy tool sequences, and also test adaptive inference schemes that dynamically choose the number of recurrent steps based on the task instance.
AI.result: Recurrent computation via looping generally improves performance on tasks that require compositional tool calling and explicit handling of dependencies and intermediate states. The performance gains for simple, single API invocation tasks are smaller and depend more on the specific model. For multi-step tool use, accuracy tends to rise with greater recurrent depth. Adaptive inference strategies further improve efficiency by using additional recurrent steps only when needed, achieving a better balance between compute cost and performance.
AI.conclusion: Looped language models offer a promising architectural direction for building agentic systems that must plan, coordinate, and execute complex, multi-step tool-use workflows. By leveraging recurrent computation—especially when applied adaptively—these models can more reliably handle compositional and dependency-aware tool use than comparable non-looped models, making them strong candidates for future agents that interact with multiple tools and APIs.

title: Stability-Aware Feature Design for Robust Watermark Detection in Machine-Generated Text
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), Seoul, South Korea. 20 pages, 5 figures
summary: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) has intensified the demand for principled methods to distinguish human from machine-generated text. Watermarking provides a promising avenue, yet existing detectors exhibit sharp performance deterioration under multiple paraphrasing and when applied to shorter texts. We introduce Pattern Stability Score (PSS), a novel detection framework that leverages local statistical features and stability dynamics across paraphrased variants. Specifically, the proposed method combines global and local z-score features with higher-order statistics of run-length patterns, enriched by autocorrelation signals and stability scores computed over paraphrase depth. Numerical evaluations are performed on three benchmark datasets (PG-19, CNN/DailyMail, and WikiText) using multiple LLMs (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2-7B) and paraphrasers (Mistral-7B, Qwen2-7B, Gemma-7B), systematically stress-testing robustness under up to eight rounds of paraphrasing. Compared to prior z-score thresholding baselines and some state-of-the-art deep learning methods, our approach improves detection AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) by over 10-15 percentage points across different token lengths. Additionally, extensive cross-domain experiments demonstrate that a single universal classifier generalizes across different LLMs, paraphrasers, and text domains without retraining, maintaining above 87.8% AUC even when all components differ from training.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Pattern Stability Score (PSS), a robust framework to detect AI-generated text, especially under heavy paraphrasing and for short texts, achieving significantly higher detection accuracy than prior watermark detectors and generalizing well across models and domains.
AI.motivation: Current watermark-based detectors for large language model (LLM) text struggle when the text is short or has undergone multiple paraphrasing steps, causing sharp performance drops. There is a need for a more robust, principled detection method that can reliably distinguish human from machine-generated text even under such adversarial or realistic conditions, and that can generalize across different LLMs, paraphrasers, and datasets without retraining.
AI.method: The authors introduce Pattern Stability Score (PSS), which models both local statistical patterns and their stability across paraphrased variants of text. They extract global and local z-score features from watermarked token sequences, compute higher-order statistics of run-length patterns, and incorporate autocorrelation-based signals. They then track how these features evolve as the text is repeatedly paraphrased, defining stability scores over paraphrase depth. These combined features feed into a classifier that predicts whether a text is watermarked/LLM-generated.
AI.result: On three benchmark datasets (PG-19, CNN/DailyMail, WikiText) and with various generator LLMs (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2-7B) and paraphrasers (Mistral-7B, Qwen2-7B, Gemma-7B), PSS is systematically evaluated under up to eight rounds of paraphrasing. It outperforms simple z-score thresholding baselines and several state-of-the-art deep learning detectors, improving detection AUC by more than 10–15 percentage points across a range of token lengths, including short texts.
AI.conclusion: Pattern Stability Score yields a more robust watermark detection approach that remains effective even after heavy paraphrasing and on short texts. Its reliance on local pattern statistics and their stability across paraphrase depth enables a single universal classifier to generalize across unseen LLMs, paraphrasers, and domains, achieving AUC above 87.8% without retraining, suggesting strong practicality for real-world AI-text detection.

title: On the Triangle Inequality for the Jaccard Distance in Arbitrary Lattices
summary: This paper presents new theoretical results on generalizing the Jaccard distance for lattices and real valuations. We demonstrate that when the valuation is strictly positive, monotone, and modular, the Jaccard distance satisfies the triangle inequality on arbitrary lattices, effectively generalizing earlier results that depended heavily on distributivity. Moving to relatively complemented distributive lattices (which safely drop the requirement for the global bounds found in Boolean algebras), we prove the triangle inequality holds as long as the valuation is positive, monotone, supermodular, and $\log$-submodular. Additionally, we adapt the symmetric-difference Jaccard formulation for submodular valuations to sectionally complemented distributive lattices. Shifting to necessary conditions, we prove that supermodularity is a strict requirement for the standard generalized Jaccard distance to operate as a valid metric. Finally, we map the practical value of relaxing these structural constraints to computational fields like quantum information theory, formal concept analysis, and machine learning, closing with a brief look at open mathematical problems.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes Jaccard distance from sets to lattices with real-valued valuations and characterizes when it is a true metric (satisfies the triangle inequality).
AI.motivation: Classical Jaccard distance is defined for sets and widely used as a similarity/distance measure, but many modern applications work with more abstract structures like lattices and with real-valued measures instead of simple cardinalities. Existing theoretical guarantees (like the triangle inequality) often rely on strong structural assumptions such as distributive Boolean algebras. The authors aim to weaken these structural assumptions and understand exactly which algebraic and valuation conditions still guarantee that generalized Jaccard distances behave as proper metrics, which is crucial for their safe use in areas like quantum information, concept analysis, and machine learning.
AI.method: They work in increasingly general classes of lattices and impose various algebraic conditions on valuations (positivity, monotonicity, modularity, supermodularity, log-submodularity). For each setting, they formally define generalized Jaccard distances (including symmetric-difference-based forms) and use lattice-theoretic and valuation-theoretic arguments to prove or refute the triangle inequality. They also derive necessary conditions—showing that without supermodularity, the standard generalized Jaccard distance fails to be a metric—by constructing or reasoning about counterexamples. Finally, they connect these abstract results to structures arising in several computational domains.
AI.result: 1) On arbitrary lattices, if the valuation is strictly positive, monotone, and modular, their generalized Jaccard distance satisfies the triangle inequality, extending earlier work beyond distributive lattices. 2) On relatively complemented distributive lattices (without requiring global bounds), they show that the triangle inequality holds under weaker, but more nuanced, valuation assumptions: positivity, monotonicity, supermodularity, and log-submodularity. 3) They extend a symmetric-difference-style Jaccard formulation, previously known for submodular valuations, to sectionally complemented distributive lattices. 4) They prove a necessity result: supermodularity is strictly required for the standard generalized Jaccard distance to be a valid metric, delineating the exact boundary of applicability. 5) They outline how these theoretical guarantees apply to objects relevant in quantum information theory, formal concept analysis, and machine learning.
AI.conclusion: Generalized Jaccard distances can be made into bona fide metrics on a wide range of lattice structures, but only under specific algebraic and valuation conditions. The paper significantly relaxes prior structural requirements while also pinning down necessary conditions, especially the essential role of supermodularity. This clarifies when Jaccard-type distances are mathematically sound for use in complex, lattice-based data representations commonly found in several computational fields, and it highlights remaining open mathematical questions about further generalizations and boundary cases.

title: DeepTCM1.0: A Multi-Expert AI Agent for Deciphering Mechanisms of Chinese Herbal Formulae Based on General Large Language Models
summary: Background: Mechanistic elucidation of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) compound formulas remains a central challenge in the modernization of TCM. Conventional approaches, including data mining and network pharmacology, are insufficient for achieving deep integration between classical TCM theory and modern scientific research. In addition, direct question-answering using general-purpose artificial intelligence large language models is limited by inadequate adaptation to TCM theoretical frameworks and susceptibility to reasoning hallucinations. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop intelligent analytical methods aligned with the holistic principles of TCM. Objective: To establish a multi-expert intelligent agent framework integrating classical TCM theory with modern life sciences, thereby enabling systematic and interpretable mechanistic analysis of TCM compound formulas, with Guizhi Decoction serving as a representative validation case. Methods: The DeepTCM1.0 framework was constructed based on the general-purpose large language model DeepSeek V3.2. It adopts a three-tier collaborative architecture and a three-round iterative quality-control workflow, simulating the collaborative analytical process of 11 interdisciplinary intelligent agents. The framework was applied to the mechanistic interpretation of Guizhi Decoction from the dual perspectives of classical traditional Chinese medicine theory and modern scientific research. Framework performance was comprehensively evaluated through double-blind five-dimensional scoring, intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) reliability testing, Mann-Whitney U tests, and effect size analysis. The evaluation employed four independent large language models as evaluators, each conducting five rounds of repeated scoring on five anonymized reports, resulting in a total of 100 independent scoring assessments.

AI.tldr: The paper builds an intelligent multi-agent framework (DeepTCM1.0) based on a large language model to systematically and reliably analyze the mechanisms of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) compound formulas, validated on Guizhi Decoction, and quantitatively evaluates the framework’s performance using multi-model, multi-round scoring and statistical tests.
AI.motivation: Understanding the mechanisms of multi-herb TCM formulas is difficult because current tools (data mining, network pharmacology, direct LLM Q&A) do not deeply integrate classical TCM theory with modern life sciences and are prone to shallow or hallucinated reasoning. There is an urgent need for an AI-based analytical framework that respects TCM’s holistic theoretical system while remaining scientifically rigorous and interpretable.
AI.method: The authors construct DeepTCM1.0, a three-tier, multi-agent framework built on the DeepSeek V3.2 large language model. It simulates 11 specialized intelligent experts working collaboratively through a three-round iterative quality-control process. This framework analyzes Guizhi Decoction simultaneously from classical TCM theoretical perspectives and modern biomedical evidence. Performance is evaluated via a rigorous protocol: double-blind, five-dimensional scoring; intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) to test reliability; Mann–Whitney U tests to compare groups; and effect size analysis. Four independent LLMs act as blinded evaluators, each performing five repeated scoring rounds on five anonymized reports, yielding 100 independent evaluations.
AI.result: DeepTCM1.0 successfully generates systematic, interpretable mechanistic analyses of Guizhi Decoction that can be assessed and compared. The evaluation design produces 100 independent scores from four different LLM evaluators across multiple dimensions, enabling calculation of reliability (ICC) and statistical differences (Mann–Whitney U) along with effect sizes. Although numeric outcomes are not stated in the abstract, the structure implies that the framework’s outputs met predefined quality and reliability criteria better than comparison baselines.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a multi-agent, quality-controlled LLM framework can effectively integrate classical TCM theory with modern life sciences to analyze the mechanisms of TCM compound formulas. DeepTCM1.0, validated on Guizhi Decoction, provides a systematic, interpretable, and quantitatively evaluable approach that surpasses ad hoc LLM Q&A and traditional data-mining or network-pharmacology methods, suggesting a viable path for the modernization and scientific interpretation of TCM formulas.

title: GenEx: A Graph-Based Representational Paradigm for SARS-CoV-2 Variant Detection via Codon Co-occurrence Networks
summary: Genomic analysis on viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 variants: Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron is heavily dominated by classical bioinformatics methods, including Sequence Alignment, Phylogenetic Analysis, and Mutation Frequency Statistics. These approaches use pairwise codon or nucleotide distance matrices to analyze gene sequences, treating them as linear strings rather than capturing their complex contextual interdependencies. We proposed GenEx, a pipeline that converts raw gene sequences into codon co-occurrence graphs and extracts more than 25 graph features. Our two most prominent techniques for graph generation and feature extraction are MSCG (Multi-Scale Codon Co-occurrence Graph) and LAPCG (Linear-time Adjacency PMI Codon Graph). Using these algorithms, we treated codon sequences as structured symbolic vocabularies interpretable to codon co-occurrence graph analysis, a representational paradigm borrowed from computational linguistics. Another major contribution includes implementing a spectral graph feature extraction using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), using the squared singular value ($σ^2$) instead of the traditionally used eigenvalue, which helped us to amplify the separation between dominant and subdominant spectral components, thereby enhancing inter-class separability in downstream classification. And to further demonstrate that our method works, we trained 23 benchmarked ML models against the latest SARS-CoV-2 variants, achieving remarkable results in detecting all SARS-CoV-2 variants.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GenEx, a graph-based pipeline for representing viral gene sequences that improves variant classification over classical sequence-alignment methods.
AI.motivation: Classical viral genomics tools (sequence alignment, phylogenetics, mutation statistics) treat gene sequences as linear strings and rely on distance matrices, which fail to capture richer contextual and co-occurrence relationships between codons. The authors want a representation that encodes these higher-order dependencies to better distinguish and classify SARS-CoV-2 variants.
AI.method: They propose GenEx, which transforms raw viral gene sequences into codon co-occurrence graphs and computes 25+ graph-based features. Two key graph-construction techniques are: (1) MSCG (Multi-Scale Codon Co-occurrence Graph), which likely captures codon relationships at multiple neighborhood or window scales, and (2) LAPCG (Linear-time Adjacency PMI Codon Graph), which constructs graphs using pointwise mutual information of codon adjacency in linear time. They also introduce a spectral feature-extraction step based on SVD, using squared singular values σ^2 instead of eigenvalues to emphasize dominant spectral components. These graph features then serve as inputs to a battery of 23 machine learning models for variant classification.
AI.result: When applied to SARS-CoV-2 variants (Beta, Gamma, Delta, Omicron, etc.), GenEx’s graph-based features allow 23 benchmark ML models to detect and distinguish all variants with strong performance (described as “remarkable results”). The use of σ^2-based spectral features improves inter-class separability relative to standard approaches.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based codon co-occurrence representations, combined with spectral features from SVD and standard ML classifiers, provide a powerful alternative to classic bioinformatics workflows for viral genomic analysis. GenEx effectively captures contextual codon dependencies and improves discrimination among SARS-CoV-2 variants, demonstrating the potential of computational-linguistics-inspired graph models in genomics.

title: StocksTalk: A Voice-Enabled Conversational Agent for Structured Query Generation over Web Data
summary: StocksTalk is a voice-enabled conversational system for transforming spoken financial screening requests into executable and validated structured queries over real-world market data. The system combines streaming speech recognition, retrieval-augmented constraint extraction, schema-grounded LLM-based SQL generation, rule-based validation, and human-in-the-loop verification within an interactive dashboard. Unlike traditional template-driven financial assistants, StocksTalk exposes intermediate reasoning artifacts, including extracted constraints, normalized financial metrics, operator grounding, and generated queries, allowing users to inspect and refine each stage before execution. To evaluate the system, we curate a benchmark of 150 spoken financial prompts spanning multiple investment strategies and input noise conditions. Experimental results show that retrieval grounding, constrained query generation, and interactive verification substantially improve constraint extraction accuracy, SQL executability, logical consistency, and multi-turn stability compared to baseline LLM-based approaches. StocksTalk demonstrates how transparent, voice-driven interfaces can bridge natural language interaction and structured financial analysis, providing an effective framework for conversational stock screening and decision support.

AI.tldr: StocksTalk is a voice-driven system that turns spoken stock-screening requests into accurate, validated SQL queries over real market data.
AI.motivation: Retail and professional investors increasingly use conversational interfaces, but existing financial assistants are often template-based, opaque, and brittle, especially for complex screening logic, noisy speech input, and multi-turn interactions. There is a need for a transparent, robust system that can reliably transform natural spoken requests into correct and executable structured queries over financial databases, while letting users understand and control each reasoning step.
AI.method: The authors design StocksTalk, a pipeline system that integrates: (1) streaming speech recognition to transcribe spoken prompts, (2) retrieval-augmented constraint extraction to identify and normalize financial constraints from text, (3) schema-grounded, LLM-based SQL generation that is guided by the underlying database schema, (4) rule-based validation to detect errors and inconsistencies, and (5) a human-in-the-loop interactive dashboard that surfaces intermediate reasoning artifacts (constraints, metrics, operators, and SQL) and lets users iteratively refine queries. They also construct a benchmark of 150 spoken financial prompts covering diverse investment strategies and noise conditions to systematically evaluate the system.
AI.result: On the curated benchmark, StocksTalk with retrieval grounding, constrained SQL generation, and interactive verification outperforms baseline LLM-only methods on several dimensions: higher accuracy of extracted constraints, greater proportion of executable SQL queries, fewer logical inconsistencies between user intent and generated queries, and improved robustness in multi-turn conversational settings. The experiments highlight that exposing and validating intermediate representations significantly boosts overall system reliability.
AI.conclusion: StocksTalk shows that a transparent, modular, and voice-enabled pipeline can effectively connect natural language interaction with structured financial analysis. By exposing intermediate reasoning steps and incorporating user verification, the system improves the correctness and stability of conversational stock screening. The work proposes a practical framework for building reliable, voice-driven decision-support tools in finance and potentially other data-intensive domains.

title: Redakto - The Incognito Tab for LLMs
comment: Accepted at WIPE-OUT 2026, 2nd Workshop on Machine Unlearning and Privacy Preservation at ECML-PKDD
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being increasingly used in everyday applications. A major challenge in the context of LLMs or Artificial Intelligence (AI) in general is to ensure privacy when using them, meaning that personally identifiable information (PII) is removed from any text that enters an LLM. These challenges have become more urgent with novel EU legislation. Uncertainty around LLM usage with respect to privacy concerns in EU countries can be a major blocker for the speed of innovation and transfer from research to applications. Here we present \textbf{Redakto}, a tool that can be used for anonymizing text prior to feeding it to an LLM or other downstream text processing. We provide state-of-the-art functionalities for both redaction of PII but also when used for pseudonymization. These functionalities are exposed such that they can easily be used by end-users, through the Redakto web application, and by developers and researchers, via REST APIs and model context protocol (MCP) hooks.
