At query time, this structure is provided to LLM agents via seven typed tools and three procedural skills integrated into a standard open-source agent harness. They run controlled experiments replacing only the action surface (tools/skills and corpus scaffold) while keeping models and harness fixed, and conduct ablations to isolate the contributions of typed structure versus procedural skills.
AI.result: On the public CTIConnect benchmark, simply swapping in CTIFoundry as the action surface yields an increase of approximately +0.19 to +0.28 overall F1 across four LLMs from two providers, compared to a flat, chunk-based substrate. A smaller model using CTIFoundry outperforms a flagship model operating on the unstructured corpus. Furthermore, the improved performance does not come from heavier search: for both Claude models, the scaffolded agent achieves higher accuracy while using roughly half as many tool calls. Ablation results show that typed structural information contributes most of the improvement, while procedural skills add further gains and interact super-additively with structure.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the primary limitation in current LLM-based CTI investigation is the corpus substrate rather than model capability. By materializing and exposing the latent structure of CTI knowledge bases as an ontology graph, span-grounded entities, and typed tools plus procedural skills, CTIFoundry enables significantly more effective and efficient agent behavior. Typed structure provides a strong backbone, procedural skills transform that structure into disciplined investigative behavior, and together they yield performance that surpasses larger models relying on conventional flat RAG. This suggests future CTI systems should prioritize agent-native corpus scaffolds to unlock the full potential of LLM agents.

title: MissDiag: Diagnostic Evaluation of Incomplete-Knowledge Robustness in KGQA and KG-RAG
summary: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) and knowledge-graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (KG-RAG) aim to ground answers in explicit graph evidence, but real-world knowledge graphs are often sparse, outdated, and incomplete. Existing robustness evaluations usually report aggregate changes in answer quality after evidence is removed or perturbed, which measures sensitivity to incomplete support but leaves the source of degradation under-specified: the same score change can conflate the type of missing evidence, the response of the evaluated system, and the sensitivity of the answer-matching protocol. To address this gap, we propose \textbf{MissDiag}, a diagnostic evaluation framework for incomplete-knowledge robustness in KGQA and KG-RAG. MissDiag keeps the question and gold answer fixed while applying structurally typed missingness interventions to benchmark-provided support graphs, enabling paired comparisons that decompose robustness changes by evidence type, system response, and evaluation protocol rather than reducing them to a single aggregate score drop. Experiments across multiple system families show that incomplete-knowledge robustness is better understood as a typed degradation phenomenon than as a uniform property: answer-adjacent evidence loss produces the largest observed degradation, source-context removal is often neutral and can be beneficial, and semantic answer matching changes absolute scores while preserving the main typed degradation patterns. By transforming aggregate robustness measurement into typed diagnostic attribution, MissDiag provides a more interpretable basis for comparing, diagnosing, and stress-testing KGQA and KG-RAG systems under incomplete knowledge.

AI.tldr: MissDiag is a diagnostic framework to analyze how different kinds of missing knowledge in a knowledge graph affect robustness of KGQA and KG-RAG systems.
AI.motivation: Existing robustness evaluations for knowledge-graph-based QA and RAG only give aggregate performance drops when evidence is removed, which mixes together multiple factors (type of missing evidence, system behavior, and evaluation protocol). This makes it unclear why performance degrades and which missingness patterns are most harmful. A more fine-grained, interpretable evaluation is needed to understand robustness under incomplete knowledge graphs.
AI.method: MissDiag keeps the question and gold answer fixed while manipulating the support subgraph with carefully designed, structurally typed missingness interventions (e.g., removing answer-adjacent evidence vs. source-context nodes). For each intervention type, it performs paired comparisons of model outputs and scores across different KGQA and KG-RAG systems and under different answer-matching protocols, allowing decomposition of robustness into contributions from evidence type, system response, and evaluation setup rather than a single scalar drop.
AI.result: Across multiple families of KGQA and KG-RAG systems, MissDiag reveals that robustness to incomplete knowledge is not uniform but depends strongly on the type of missing evidence: removing answer-adjacent evidence causes the largest degradation in answer quality, removing more peripheral source-context information is often neutral or even helpful, and changing from exact to semantic answer matching shifts absolute performance levels but preserves the qualitative patterns of typed degradation uncovered by the framework.
AI.conclusion: MissDiag turns coarse robustness scores into a diagnostic attribution over evidence types, model behaviors, and evaluation settings. This more interpretable, typed view of degradation enables more meaningful comparison, debugging, and stress testing of KGQA and KG-RAG systems operating over incomplete knowledge graphs.

title: Preference Reasoning under Indeterminacy in Large Language Models
comment: 55 pages, 14 figures
summary: As large language models evolve into decision-making agents, the ability to reason over preferences becomes fundamental to alignment, coordination, and collective intelligence. Yet, unlike standard benchmarks, real-world preference reasoning is inherently indeterminate: information may be incomplete, and valid solutions may not exist. We argue that indeterminacy, rather than correctness alone, is a central challenge for AI reasoning. We formalize this challenge along two axes, (i) epistemic indeterminacy, arising from incomplete, partial, or expressive preferences, and (ii) structural indeterminacy, arising from the non-existence of solutions under standard social choice concepts. Across a hierarchy of tasks, we show that state-of-the-art language models systematically fail to distinguish between determined and undetermined instances, exhibiting miscalibrated reasoning even in verification settings.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the key challenge for AI preference reasoning is handling indeterminate cases, not just getting determinate answers correct, and shows that current LLMs systematically fail to recognize when preferences are under- or ill-defined.
AI.motivation: As large language models are increasingly used as decision-making agents in alignment, coordination, and collective intelligence settings, they must reason over human or multi-agent preferences. In real-world scenarios, such preferences are often incomplete, only partially specified, or mutually incompatible, such that no standard social choice solution exists. Existing benchmarks mostly assume well-defined, fully determined problems, so there is a gap between benchmark performance and the messy, indeterminate nature of real preference reasoning. The paper is motivated by understanding and formalizing this gap and diagnosing whether current LLMs can detect and appropriately respond to such indeterminacy.
AI.method: The authors conceptually distinguish two types of indeterminacy in preference reasoning: (i) epistemic indeterminacy, caused by incomplete, partial, or rich but under-specified preference descriptions, and (ii) structural indeterminacy, caused by the impossibility of finding a solution under standard social choice notions (e.g., no option satisfies all axioms). They then construct a hierarchy of tasks that instantiate these forms of indeterminacy and evaluate state-of-the-art language models on them. The tasks include both problem-solving and verification-style questions, where models must either find a solution or correctly recognize that a situation is underdetermined or unsolvable according to the given criteria. They analyze model outputs to assess whether models can distinguish determined from undetermined instances and whether their confidence is calibrated to the actual determinacy of the problems.
AI.result: Across the hierarchy of tasks, current state-of-the-art language models perform poorly at recognizing when preference reasoning problems are indeterminate. They frequently propose definitive solutions in cases where, by construction, the instance is underdetermined or has no valid solution under the specified social choice criteria. Even when placed in verification roles, where they only need to confirm or deny proposed solutions, their judgments remain miscalibrated: they often treat undetermined instances as if they were determined, and vice versa. This reveals a systematic failure to distinguish determined from undetermined cases, rather than occasional random errors.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that indeterminacy is a central, under-addressed challenge for AI reasoning about preferences. Simply optimizing models for correctness on well-posed benchmarks is insufficient, because real-world decision-making involves incomplete information and structural impossibilities. The inability of current LLMs to recognize and appropriately respond to epistemic and structural indeterminacy indicates a form of miscalibrated reasoning that threatens reliable alignment and coordination. The authors imply that future work should explicitly model and train for recognition of indeterminacy, uncertainty-aware inference, and more nuanced treatment of preference data and social choice constraints, rather than assuming that every problem admits a single correct solution.

title: DART-SD: Diamond-topology Aware Retrieval and Tuning for Self-Distillation of Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents
summary: Equipping Large Language Models (LLMs) with multi-turn tool-calling capabilities is essential for building autonomous agents. However, progress is fundamentally limited by the reliance on full-length trajectory imitation. For tasks involving multiple order-independent sub-goals, the optimal solution space forms a vast combinatorial diamond lattice. Forcing this rich topology into monolithic trajectories causes a severe topological collapse, indiscriminately penalizing valid alternative explorations and severely degrading policy diversity. To address this, we propose DART-SD (Diamond-topology Aware Retrieval and Tuning for Self-Distillation), a novel framework that shifts the paradigm from global forcing to topology-guided localized correction. DART-SD first models the execution process as a converging Interaction-State Transition Graph (ISTG), faithfully capturing the inherent diamond topology of successful and failed exploratory paths. During autonomous rollouts, the framework identifies the Critical Topological Breakpoint (CTB) and retrieves success-supported recovery references. Finally, we introduce a progressive self-distillation paradigm through CTB-guided localized supervision, ensuring that the training loss is calculated exclusively on the generated recovery steps while strictly protecting the valid reasoning prefix from destructive gradient updates. Experiments on complex multi-turn tool-calling benchmarks demonstrate that DART-SD significantly outperforms traditional full-trajectory baselines.

AI.tldr: DART-SD is a training framework that improves multi-turn tool-calling LLM agents by avoiding full-trajectory imitation and instead applying localized corrections based on the problem’s diamond-shaped solution topology.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous LLM agents for multi-turn tool use are trained via full-length trajectory imitation. For tasks with multiple order-independent sub-goals, many different action orders are valid, forming a combinatorial diamond-like solution space. Full-trajectory supervision collapses this structure into a single path, penalizing other valid exploration patterns, reducing policy diversity, and harming performance. A method is needed that respects this topology and updates models without destroying valid reasoning prefixes.
AI.method: The authors model the agent’s multi-turn interaction as an Interaction-State Transition Graph (ISTG) that explicitly encodes both successful and failed exploratory paths and reveals the underlying diamond topology. During autonomous rollouts, they detect a Critical Topological Breakpoint (CTB) where the trajectory diverges from success-supporting paths. They then retrieve reference recovery trajectories that successfully navigate past similar CTBs. Training uses a progressive self-distillation scheme that applies supervision only to the recovery steps after the CTB while freezing or protecting the prefix steps that are already valid, thus shifting from global trajectory forcing to localized, topology-aware correction.
AI.result: On complex multi-turn tool-calling benchmarks, DART-SD achieves significantly better performance than standard full-trajectory imitation baselines. The framework improves success rates on tasks requiring multiple order-independent sub-goals and enhances policy robustness and diversity in tool-use strategies.
AI.conclusion: Respecting the diamond-like topology of multi-step tool-use tasks and applying supervision only at critical breakpoints allows LLM agents to learn more effective, diverse, and robust tool-calling behaviors. DART-SD’s ISTG modeling, CTB detection, and localized self-distillation form a general framework that overcomes the topological collapse induced by monolithic trajectory imitation, leading to state-of-the-art results on challenging multi-turn tool-calling benchmarks.

title: Candidate-Fate Accounting for Transparent Sensor Diagnostic Pipeline Search
summary: Industrial sensor diagnostics relies on preprocessing, representation, and classification pipelines, making automated pipeline search useful for reducing manual design cost. However, existing automated machine/deep learning (AutoML/AutoDL) reports typically retain only fitted trials, scores, and winners, omitting generated candidates that are invalid, pruned, skipped, cached, or unfitted. This omission limits reviewers' ability to check signal constraints, budget use, and unevaluated legal alternatives. To address this, we propose candidate-fate accounting, a candidate-level audit framework for diagnostic search traces. It records each observed candidate as auditable evidence: hashes merge repeated observations, legality checks flag invalid candidates, allocation rationales explain budget decisions, and a closed fate ledger assigns one terminal fate to each candidate. Experiments on three bearing-diagnostic datasets show that the framework detects invalid candidates and identifies 30--41 candidates omitted by fitted-trial-only reports, with closed fate records verifying complete candidate accounting while maintaining competitive diagnostic performance. The code is available at https://github.com/XXIE999/candidate-fate-accounting.

AI.tldr: They introduce an auditing framework for AutoML/AutoDL pipelines in industrial sensor diagnostics that records the fate of every candidate pipeline, not just the ones that get fitted, to ensure completeness, validity checks, and transparent use of resources.
AI.motivation: Current industrial sensor diagnostic systems use automated search over preprocessing, feature representation, and classification pipelines. Existing AutoML/AutoDL reports only keep information about successfully fitted trials and their scores, ignoring many generated candidates that are invalid, skipped, pruned, or never fitted. This lack of full trace information prevents reviewers from verifying whether signal constraints were respected, how the computational budget was allocated, and whether promising but unevaluated legal alternatives were overlooked. The authors want a way to fully audit search behavior and candidate handling.
AI.method: They propose "candidate-fate accounting," a candidate-level audit framework for AutoML/AutoDL search traces in industrial diagnostics. For every candidate pipeline observed during the search, the framework stores auditable evidence: (1) a hash-based mechanism to merge and track repeated observations of the same candidate; (2) legality checks that mark invalid candidates; (3) allocation rationales explaining why certain candidates did or did not receive computational budget; and (4) a closed fate ledger that assigns exactly one terminal fate (such as fitted, pruned, invalid, skipped, cached, or unfitted) to each candidate. This yields a complete, structured log of the search process.
AI.result: On three bearing-diagnostic datasets, the framework: (1) successfully detects invalid candidates; (2) reveals 30–41 candidates that would be omitted if one only reported fitted trials, showing the extent of hidden search behavior; and (3) keeps diagnostic performance competitive with standard approaches, indicating that the additional auditing does not harm the effectiveness of the resulting diagnostic pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Candidate-fate accounting enables complete and transparent auditing of AutoML/AutoDL diagnostic pipeline searches by systematically recording the fate of every candidate. It uncovers hidden invalid or unevaluated candidates, provides verifiable evidence of budget allocation and legality checks, and does so without sacrificing diagnostic performance. This makes automated diagnostic systems more trustworthy and reviewable in industrial sensor settings.

title: Shared Circuits for Shared Grammar: Tracing Subject-Verb Agreement Across Languages
comment: 25 pages including appendices, 16 figures. Accepted to COLM 2026
summary: Multilingual large language models often generalize across languages, and prior work suggests that their internal mechanisms can overlap cross-lingually. It remains unclear, however, when such sharing emerges and whether it varies with the overt realization of the same grammatical operation. We investigate this question for present-tense subject-verb agreement, a morphosyntactic process that varies substantially across languages and is only weakly expressed in English. Using activation patching and attention analysis across 29 languages and five open-source model families, we identify the attention heads causally implicated in agreement and compare these head-level signatures across languages. We find that languages with overt person/number inflection exhibit more similar agreement circuitry than non-conjugating languages, with the strongest sharing appearing when the analysis isolates recovery of the inflectional contrast itself. English provides an informative bridge case, becoming more similar to conjugating languages precisely in contexts where overt agreement is required. Finally, many implicated heads display similar attention patterns across languages, suggesting that cross-lingual overlap reflects shared functional roles as well as shared localization. Together, these results indicate that multilingual LLMs reuse partially shared computational structure for morphosyntactic agreement rather than relying on fully separate language-specific solutions.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how multilingual large language models internally implement subject-verb agreement across many languages and shows that models partially reuse shared neural circuitry, especially in languages with overt agreement inflection.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs can generalize across languages, but it is not well understood when and how their internal mechanisms are shared cross-lingually. In particular, morphosyntactic processes like subject-verb agreement differ widely in how overtly they are realized across languages and are weakly marked in English. The authors want to know whether models use shared or language-specific mechanisms for such agreement, and how this depends on the presence of explicit inflectional morphology.
AI.method: The authors analyze present-tense subject-verb agreement in 29 languages using five open-source multilingual LLM families. They employ activation patching to causally identify attention heads responsible for agreement, and perform attention pattern analysis to characterize which heads are involved and how. They then compare these head-level causal and attention signatures across languages, looking at variation based on whether a language has overt person/number inflection and at contexts that specifically require overt agreement marking.
AI.result: They find that languages with overt person/number inflection share more similar agreement-related circuitry than languages without conjugation. The strongest cross-lingual sharing appears when the analysis targets recovery of the inflectional contrast itself. English acts as a bridge: its internal mechanisms become more similar to those of conjugating languages precisely in contexts where explicit agreement is required. Additionally, many causally implicated attention heads exhibit similar attention patterns across languages.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs do not learn entirely separate, language-specific solutions for morphosyntactic agreement. Instead, they reuse partially shared computational structure and attention circuitry across languages, especially those with overt inflectional morphology. Cross-lingual overlap reflects both shared localization (which heads are involved) and shared functional roles (how those heads attend), highlighting systematic internal generalization for subject-verb agreement in multilingual models.

title: Sanyu Studio: A Multi-Agent System for Art-Historical Narrative Construction
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables
summary: Amid concerns that generative AI may standardize art interpretation, this paper examines whether LLM-based interaction can support plural art-historical narrative construction. We present Sanyu Studio, a multi-agent dialogue system that models 321 Sanyu oil paintings as agents with fact, interpretation, organization, and memory-filtering mechanisms. Based on a seven-day workshop with eight art-university participants, the study shows that user prompts, evidence organization, and cognitive tendencies shaped divergent yet coherent versions of digital Sanyu. The findings suggest that, under conditions of limited historical evidence, AI can amplify human agency and offer public audiences an interactive entry point into art-historical interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a multi-agent LLM system, Sanyu Studio, to treat 321 paintings by the artist Sanyu as interactive agents and studies whether such AI interaction can support multiple, divergent but coherent art-historical narratives instead of a single standardized interpretation.
AI.motivation: There is a concern that generative AI might homogenize or standardize how art is interpreted, potentially suppressing plural perspectives. The authors want to investigate whether LLM-based systems can instead foster multiple, coexisting art-historical narratives, especially in cases where historical evidence about an artist is scarce and interpretation plays a central role.
AI.method: The authors design Sanyu Studio, a multi-agent dialogue system where each of 321 Sanyu oil paintings is modeled as an agent. These agents incorporate mechanisms for factual information, interpretive reasoning, organization of evidence, and memory filtering. They then run a seven-day workshop with eight art-university participants who interact with the system, and they analyze how users’ prompts, evidence organization, and cognitive tendencies shape the resulting narratives about Sanyu.
AI.result: The workshop shows that different users, through their own prompting strategies, ways of organizing evidence, and personal cognitive tendencies, create divergent yet internally coherent narrative versions of “digital Sanyu.” This indicates that the system does not push everyone toward a single standardized account but instead supports plural interpretations.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that, particularly when historical evidence about an artist is limited, LLM-based multi-agent systems like Sanyu Studio can enhance human agency in interpretation and provide public audiences with an interactive way to engage in art-historical narrative construction, supporting plural, coexisting readings rather than a single canonical one.

title: Beyond LLM-Based Reasoning: Lightweight GNNs for Agent Failure Attribution
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) often exhibit complex failure modes, which frequently cause agents to produce incorrect outcomes. This motivates the task of Agent Failure Attribution: given a failed multi-agent trajectory, identify the faulty agents and their corresponding error types. Existing approaches predominantly rely on LLMs to perform failure attribution, either through direct prompting, fine-tuning on synthetic data or complex agentic pipelines. While effective, these methods incur substantial computational overhead due to long-context processing, expensive post-training and handcrafted workflows. Moreover, empirical evidence shows that even state-of-the-art models achieve limited accuracy on existing benchmarks, suggesting that scaling model size alone is insufficient. In this work, we revisit this task and question the necessity of such expensive generative solutions. We introduce AFANet, a lightweight graph-based framework that models interaction trajectories through step-level semantic signals and agent-level relationships. We show that with significantly fewer parameters and near-zero inference cost, AFANet (i) matches or outperforms LLM-based baselines, including fine-tuned models on in-domain benchmarks, (ii) maintains robust performance across different GNN architectures and (iii) can be further improved with inexpensive test-time adaptation on the OOD benchmark. Our results suggest that effective agent failure attribution does not require heavy LLM reasoning and a lightweight, structured approach can achieve strong performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AFANet, a lightweight graph-based method for attributing failures in LLM-based multi-agent systems, achieving comparable or better performance than LLM-centric approaches with far lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems frequently fail in complex ways, and identifying which agents failed and why (agent failure attribution) is important. Existing methods rely heavily on large LLMs via prompting, fine-tuning, or elaborate agent pipelines, which are computationally expensive and still inaccurate, suggesting that simply scaling LLMs is not enough. The paper aims to find a more efficient and accurate alternative.
AI.method: The authors formulate agent failure attribution as a graph learning problem. They design AFANet, a graph-based framework that represents multi-agent interaction trajectories with step-level semantic signals (capturing what happens at each step) and agent-level relationships (capturing how agents interact). AFANet is implemented with graph neural networks (GNNs) and is intentionally lightweight in terms of parameter count and inference cost. They test it across different GNN variants and evaluate it on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks.
AI.result: AFANet, despite having far fewer parameters and very low inference cost compared to LLM-based approaches, matches or outperforms strong LLM baselines, including models that were fine-tuned specifically for this task. Its performance remains robust across different choices of GNN architectures. Additionally, on out-of-distribution benchmarks, AFANet can be further improved using inexpensive test-time adaptation techniques.
AI.conclusion: Agent failure attribution in multi-agent LLM systems does not require heavy generative reasoning from large language models. Instead, a lightweight, structured graph-based approach like AFANet can achieve strong and robust performance at a fraction of the computational cost. This challenges the assumption that larger or more complex LLM-based solutions are necessary for this task and highlights the value of structured modeling of interactions.

title: RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training
summary: Training multi-turn agentic workflows with reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models to perform complex reasoning, use external tools, and conduct iterative search beyond single-turn settings. Yet multi-turn RL training remains highly unstable, often causing severe performance degradation as the number of turns increases. Through theoretical analysis, we identify three tightly coupled sources of instability: rollout-training context mismatch, weak turn-level credit assignment under sparse terminal rewards, and asynchronous policy drift when short and long trajectories are optimized under different policy versions. We show that these issues share a common structural origin in flattened trajectory optimization and address them through a unified reverse-turn formulation. We propose Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization (RTPO), which organizes multi-turn rollouts as sparse reverse trees and performs turn-level policy updates in temporal reverse order, aligning each decision with its downstream continuation. RTPO enables causally consistent turn-level credit assignment and on-policy continuation to control asynchronous drift. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that RTPO eliminates context mismatch and asynchronous drift under the proposed turn-level formulation, reduces credit bias, and converges to recursive optimality. Experiments on multi-turn agentic RL benchmarks show that RTPO improves upon trajectory- and turn-level baselines by 21.50% and 10.76%, respectively, highlighting its potential to support more stable training for tool-using agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization (RTPO), a reinforcement learning method that stabilizes multi-turn training of tool-using language agents by restructuring trajectory optimization in reverse-turn order.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn RL for large language model agents is powerful but unstable: performance often degrades as conversation length grows. The authors observe three main problems—context mismatch between rollout and training, poor turn-level credit assignment under sparse rewards, and policy drift when different parts of trajectories are optimized under different policy versions. These issues limit the reliability and scalability of current multi-turn agent training.
AI.method: The authors analyze the instability as arising from a flattened trajectory optimization perspective and propose a unified reverse-turn formulation. They introduce Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization (RTPO), which restructures multi-turn rollouts into sparse reverse trees and performs policy updates from the final turns backward. Each decision is updated using its actual downstream continuation under a consistent policy, enabling causally aligned turn-level credit assignment and on-policy continuation. They provide a theoretical framework showing how this reverse-turn scheme removes context mismatch and asynchronous drift and reduces credit bias while converging to a recursively optimal policy.
AI.result: Theoretically, RTPO is proven to eliminate rollout-training context mismatch and asynchronous policy drift in the proposed formulation, improve turn-level credit assignment, and converge to recursive optimality. Empirically, on multi-turn agentic RL benchmarks (e.g., tool-using agents and multi-step reasoning tasks), RTPO yields substantial performance gains: an average 21.50% improvement over trajectory-level baselines and 10.76% over existing turn-level baselines, demonstrating more stable and effective multi-turn training.
AI.conclusion: RTPO provides a principled and practical solution to instability in multi-turn RL training for LLM-based agents by reorganizing optimization in reverse-turn order. This reverse-turn framework offers better credit assignment, eliminates key sources of drift and mismatch, and yields strong empirical gains, suggesting it can serve as a robust foundation for training complex, tool-using conversational agents in longer-horizon settings.

title: Compress and Forget: bitsandbytes Quantization Amplifies Proactive Interference in LLMs
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Code and data released at https://github.com/ShayanShahrabi/compress-and-forget
summary: Proactive interference (PI) is a documented failure mode in large language models in which retrieval of a repeatedly overwritten value degrades as prior overwrites accumulate, mirroring a classical phenomenon in human working memory. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is now the default deployment path for open-weight models, yet its effect on this failure mode has not been tested. We evaluate three precision levels (FP16, INT8, INT4/NF4, via bitsandbytes) across three architecturally distinct instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Phi-3.5-mini-instruct), holding the retrieval task fixed. INT4 quantization significantly reduces accuracy under high interference in every model (e.g., from 81.0% to 68.3% for Qwen), confirmed by paired McNemar's tests ($p \le 2.6 \times 10^{-6}$) and a mixed-effects regression spanning all interference levels; INT8, often assumed safe, also carries a smaller but real penalty in two of three models. The effect is specific to semantically similar (word-type) distractors and reverses sign under a numeric control condition, and is mechanistically linked to a rise in same-key intrusion errors under INT4 (from 21.5% to 24.6% of trials, $p = 4.8 \times 10^{-7}$). A follow-up ablation shows the effect originates in the quantized transformer backbone rather than the output projection layer. These results suggest that bitsandbytes 4-bit quantization can impose an additional cost on applications relying on long, updatable, semantically dense contexts, even when aggregate benchmark accuracy appears largely unaffected. We release our code and tokenizer-verified vocabulary construction method at https://github.com/ShayanShahrabi/compress-and-forget

AI.tldr: The paper studies how post-training quantization (especially 4‑bit) affects proactive interference (a specific memory failure) in LLMs and finds that low-precision quantization significantly worsens this failure mode even when standard benchmarks look fine.
AI.motivation: Large language models show proactive interference: difficulty reliably retrieving a value that has been repeatedly overwritten in context, similar to human working memory failures. At the same time, post‑training quantization (PTQ), particularly to 8‑ and 4‑bit, is now standard for deploying open‑weight models to reduce memory and compute costs. However, it is unknown how quantization affects this specific failure mode, especially under long, semantically dense, updatable contexts that many applications rely on. The motivation is to test whether quantization, beyond its known small impact on aggregate benchmarks, has a targeted, potentially severe effect on interference-sensitive retrieval behavior.
AI.method: The authors evaluate proactive interference behavior in three different instruction‑tuned LLMs (Qwen2.5‑7B‑Instruct, Mistral‑7B‑Instruct‑v0.3, Phi‑3.5‑mini‑instruct) under a controlled retrieval task where a key–value mapping is repeatedly overwritten in context. They compare three precision regimes obtained via bitsandbytes PTQ: FP16 (unquantized baseline), INT8, and 4‑bit (INT4/NF4). They manipulate interference by varying the number and type of overwrites, using semantically similar word‑type distractors versus a numeric control condition. They measure retrieval accuracy and characterize specific error types, especially same‑key intrusions. Statistical analysis includes paired McNemar’s tests for model‑wise comparisons and mixed‑effects regression across all interference levels. An ablation isolates whether the performance degradation arises from quantizing the transformer backbone versus the output projection layer.
AI.result: Across all three models, 4‑bit quantization significantly reduces retrieval accuracy under high proactive interference compared to FP16; for example, Qwen accuracy drops from 81.0% to 68.3%, with highly significant McNemar’s test p‑values (≤ 2.6×10⁻⁶) and corroborating mixed‑effects regression. INT8 quantization, often assumed nearly lossless, shows a smaller but statistically meaningful performance penalty in two of the three models. The degradation is specific to semantically similar, word‑type distractors and not observed—or is reversed—in a numeric control condition. Mechanistically, INT4 models display an increased rate of same‑key intrusion errors (e.g., from 21.5% to 24.6% of trials, p = 4.8×10⁻⁷), indicating that the model more often retrieves a competing value associated with the same key. Ablation experiments indicate that the primary source of these effects is quantization of the transformer backbone rather than the output projection layer.
AI.conclusion: Post‑training quantization, especially to 4‑bit using bitsandbytes, exacerbates a known LLM failure mode—proactive interference—particularly in settings with long, semantically dense, and frequently updated contexts. Even when overall benchmark scores remain similar, quantized models can be significantly less reliable at context‑sensitive retrieval, with characteristic increases in same‑key intrusion errors. INT8 also introduces non‑negligible degradation in some models. The findings warn practitioners that aggressive PTQ can impose hidden cognitive costs on interference‑prone tasks and suggest that evaluations of quantized models should include targeted tests of interference and contextual memory, not just aggregate accuracy. The authors release code and a tokenizer‑verified vocabulary construction procedure to facilitate replication and further study.

title: Competence, Not Accuracy: A Diagnostic for Reference-Free Judge Gates in Skill Optimization
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables
summary: Text-space skill optimization adapts a frozen agent by evolving a natural-language skill document, accepting each candidate through a validation gate. Existing gates rely on verifiable rewards, confining these methods to tasks with an automatic verifier. Replacing the verifier with an LLM-judge gate would lift that restriction, but whether such a gate carries usable signal is untested. We ask a prior question: can we tell, before placing a judge in the loop, whether its scores separate correct from incorrect answers at all? We formalize a reference-free judge as a latent solver -- its verdict rests on agreement with whatever it would itself conclude, so its capacity to evaluate is bounded by its capacity to solve. The model yields a closed-form bound on discriminability (ROC-AUC) in the judge's competence $c$ and answer-space size $k$, a necessary condition $c > 1/k$, and the result that the marginal AUC is confounded by item difficulty while a within-question estimator is not. A non-intervening probe records judge scores on genuine optimization runs without altering any decision. We find discriminability at chance where competence sits near the floor and usable above it; that a judge's benchmark accuracy overstates the competence that matters; and, in a closed-loop study, that the screen predicts which kind of gating error occurs. The result is a cheap pre-deployment diagnostic for judge gates.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and how a reference-free LLM judge can reliably distinguish correct from incorrect answers, providing a theoretical framework and empirical diagnostics for judge-based validation gates in text-space skill optimization.
AI.motivation: Text-space skill optimization requires a validation gate to accept or reject evolved natural-language skills. Existing methods rely on automatic verifiers and thus are limited to tasks with explicit, verifiable rewards. Using an LLM as a judge would broaden applicability, but it is unclear whether such a judge provides a meaningful signal — i.e., whether its scores actually separate correct from incorrect answers. The authors want a way to predict this, without running expensive closed-loop experiments, before deploying an LLM judge in the optimization pipeline.
AI.method: The authors formalize a reference-free LLM judge as a latent solver whose judgments are effectively based on what it would itself answer. They derive a theoretical model that links the judge’s competence (probability of solving correctly) and the size of the answer space to an upper bound on discriminability, quantified by ROC-AUC. They obtain conditions such as a necessary competence threshold c > 1/k and analyze why marginal AUC is confounded by item difficulty, proposing a within-question estimator that avoids this. Empirically, they use a non-intervening probe: they record judge scores on real optimization runs without letting these scores influence the decisions, then analyze the scores offline to estimate discriminability. They also run a closed-loop study to see how judge quality relates to different kinds of gating errors.
AI.result: The theory yields a closed-form bound on discriminability (ROC-AUC) in terms of the judge’s competence and the number of plausible answers, and identifies c > 1/k as a necessary condition for useful discrimination. It also shows that marginal AUC can be misleading due to difficulty confounds, while a within-question estimator is more robust. Empirically, when the judge’s competence is near the minimal level, its discriminability is at chance; once competence clears this floor, the judge provides usable signal. They find that standard benchmark accuracy exaggerates the competence relevant for judging, and that their proposed screening method predicts which type of gating error (e.g., accepting bad or rejecting good candidates) will arise in closed-loop optimization.
AI.conclusion: A reference-free LLM judge can only be a useful gate for text-space skill optimization if its effective competence exceeds a task-dependent floor, which can be predicted from theory. The authors’ discriminability analysis and non-intervening probe provide a cheap pre-deployment diagnostic: by estimating within-question AUC from passive scores, practitioners can determine whether an LLM judge is likely to make helpful or harmful gating decisions before integrating it into the optimization loop.

title: From Storage to Access: Verifiable Activation of Parametric Knowledge in LLMs via Explicit Priming and Implicit Reasoning
summary: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) encode rich factual knowledge in their parameters, reliably recalling and verifying such knowledge remains a key bottleneck in factual question answering. Existing end-to-end methods entangle knowledge elicitation with reasoning, making it difficult to determine whether correct answers arise from parametric knowledge or the input context. To address this challenge, we propose VAKE (Verifiable Activation of Parametric KnowledgE), a two-stage reinforcement-learning framework that externalizes latent parametric knowledge through explicit Priming and transfers the acquired elicitation capability to implicit Reasoning. Given a query and an insufficient retrieved subgraph, the Priming policy explicitly inserts bridging triples as verifiable evidence, with supervision provided by rewards derived from answers generated by a separate frozen model over the augmented subgraph. Building on the policy learned during Priming, the Reasoning stage trains the model to answer from the original input, testing whether the capability acquired through explicit knowledge elicitation transfers to implicit reasoning. Experiments across seven benchmarks and models from 3B to 14B show that VAKE consistently outperforms standard baselines, including when transferring directly from HotpotQA to OOD datasets. LLM-based evaluation further shows that over 80% of the inserted triples provide factual bridging knowledge not derivable from the retrieved context, while more than half elicit knowledge inaccessible through direct prompting. These results suggest that VAKE activates latent parametric knowledge rather than copying the input context or memorizing dataset-specific associations.

AI.tldr: VAKE is a two-stage RL framework that first teaches a model to insert verifiable knowledge-bridging triples into a retrieved subgraph, then transfers this capability to answer from the original input, thus activating latent parametric knowledge instead of just copying context.
AI.motivation: LLMs contain factual knowledge in their parameters but struggle to reliably recall and verify it in QA tasks, and current methods entangle knowledge retrieval with reasoning so it is unclear whether correct answers come from the model’s own knowledge or from input context. The authors want a way to cleanly elicit, verify, and reuse parametric knowledge for reasoning.
AI.method: They design VAKE, a two-stage reinforcement learning approach with Priming and Reasoning. In Priming, given a query and an incomplete retrieved subgraph, a policy learns to insert explicit bridging triples as additional evidence. Rewards come from answers produced by a separate frozen model that operates only on the augmented subgraph, ensuring the triples are verifiable. In the Reasoning stage, the model is trained to answer questions from the original (unaugmented) input while reusing the previously learned Priming policy, testing whether the skill of eliciting parametric knowledge transfers to implicit reasoning. They evaluate across seven QA benchmarks and a range of LLM sizes (3B–14B), including cross-dataset transfer from HotpotQA to out-of-distribution datasets, and analyze the factuality and novelty of inserted triples with LLM-based evaluation.
AI.result: VAKE consistently achieves higher QA performance than standard baselines across seven benchmarks and model sizes from 3B to 14B parameters, including in zero-shot transfer from HotpotQA to out-of-distribution datasets. LLM evaluators indicate that over 80% of the inserted triples add factual bridging knowledge not obtainable from the retrieved context alone, and more than half of these triples elicit knowledge that cannot be accessed through direct prompting of the base model.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully externalizes and activates latent parametric knowledge via verifiable bridging triples and transfers this elicitation capability to implicit reasoning, improving factual QA. The evidence suggests VAKE is not merely copying context or memorizing dataset patterns but genuinely leveraging internal knowledge, providing a more interpretable and robust way to use parametric knowledge in LLMs.

title: A Multi-Agent Platform for Automated Enterprise Analytics and Insight Generation
summary: This paper proposes a multi-agent framework built on CrewAI [1] for conversational business intelligence. Five specialized AI agents operate in a sequential pipeline to process natural language queries, retrieve and analyze data, generate visualizations via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [2], and deliver actionable insights. The platform features a defense-in-depth security architecture for multi-tenant data isolation and a query parameterization mechanism for transforming conversational insights into reusable dashboard components. Evaluation across 300 end-to-end test cases spanning synthetic and production enterprise datasets demonstrates 95.3% functional accuracy, a mean response latency of 24 seconds, and a response quality score of 4.52/5.0 as assessed by an LLM-as-a-Judge framework, with a 93.0% hallucination-free rate, representing a 22.6 percentage point accuracy improvement and 20.2% quality gain over a single-agent baseline. Cross-model evaluation across four LLM backends and human expert validation confirm architectural generalizability and evaluator reliability. An ablation study confirms that the Data Analysis and Report Aggregation agents are the primary drivers of output quality.

AI.tldr: A paper introduces a multi-agent CrewAI-based framework for conversational business intelligence that significantly outperforms a single-agent baseline in accuracy, response quality, and hallucination reduction.
AI.motivation: Traditional single-agent LLM systems for business intelligence struggle with complex query decomposition, reliable data analysis, and hallucination control, especially in multi-tenant enterprise settings. There is a need for a more modular, robust, and secure architecture that can handle natural language queries, work across datasets, generate visualizations, and produce trustworthy, reusable analytical outputs.
AI.method: The authors design a sequential pipeline of five specialized AI agents built on CrewAI. Each agent handles a distinct stage: understanding the natural language query, retrieving relevant data, performing data analysis, generating visualizations through MCP, and aggregating results into actionable insights. The platform includes a defense-in-depth security model for multi-tenant isolation and query parameterization to turn conversational outputs into reusable dashboard components. They evaluate the system on 300 end-to-end test cases over synthetic and real enterprise datasets, compare against a single-agent baseline, run cross-model tests on four different LLMs, and perform an ablation study to assess the contribution of each agent type.
AI.result: The system achieves 95.3% functional accuracy, an average response latency of 24 seconds, a response quality score of 4.52/5.0 under an LLM-as-a-Judge setup, and a 93.0% hallucination-free rate. Compared to a single-agent baseline, it delivers a 22.6 percentage point improvement in accuracy and a 20.2% gain in response quality. Cross-model and human expert evaluations confirm that the architecture generalizes across LLM backends and that the evaluation method is reliable. The ablation study shows that the Data Analysis and Report Aggregation agents contribute most to the final output quality.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent CrewAI-based architecture is an effective and generalizable approach for conversational business intelligence, providing higher accuracy, better perceived quality, fewer hallucinations, and robust security and reusability features compared to single-agent systems. The most critical components for quality are the agents responsible for data analysis and report aggregation.

title: TranslatePsy-AfriSLM: High-Quality Data Scaling For Low-Resource Machine Translation
comment: EMNLP 2026 (under ARR, meta review of 4, awaiting accept decision)
summary: The rapid progress in Artificial Intelligence has largely bypassed African languages, creating a digital divide that limits AI adoption on the continent. Recent open-source LLMs systematically underperform on African machine translation, while the lack of large-scale, high-quality, open-source parallel data has constrained the development of competitive small language models (SLMs). We introduce *TranslatePsy-AfriSLM*, a collection of open-source MT resources for 19 Sub-Saharan African languages, including curated parallel data, African-specialized synthetic data, and a family of fine-tuned SLMs. Our empirical study shows that unified quality-estimation filtering removes up to 96% of training tokens without degrading quality, and that filtered synthetic data dominates the quality-efficiency Pareto frontier. Fine-tuned on the resulting data mixture, TranslatePsy-AfriSLM outperforms substantially larger systems, including TranslateGemma-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, with as few as 0.8B parameters.

AI.tldr: TranslatePsy-AfriSLM releases data and small translation models for 19 Sub-Saharan African languages, using aggressive quality-estimation filtering and synthetic data to beat much larger LLMs.
AI.motivation: AI progress has largely skipped African languages, causing a digital divide and weak performance of current open-source LLMs on African machine translation. A key bottleneck is the lack of large-scale, high-quality, open-source parallel data, which prevents building strong yet efficient small language models tailored to these languages.
AI.method: The authors construct TranslatePsy-AfriSLM, which includes (1) curated parallel corpora for 19 Sub-Saharan African languages, (2) African-focused synthetic translation data, and (3) a series of fine-tuned small language models. They apply a unified quality-estimation filtering pipeline to the training data—both real and synthetic—to remove low-quality segments, and then fine-tune SLMs on mixtures dominated by filtered synthetic data. They evaluate translation quality and efficiency against larger baseline systems.
AI.result: Unified quality-estimation filtering can discard up to 96% of training tokens without hurting translation quality. After filtering, synthetic data becomes the main driver of performance, occupying the best quality–efficiency trade-off compared to other data mixtures. The resulting fine-tuned TranslatePsy-AfriSLM models, with as few as 0.8B parameters, outperform substantially larger models such as TranslateGemma-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on African MT benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: High-quality, filtered synthetic data combined with curated parallel resources enables compact small language models that outperform much larger systems for African machine translation. TranslatePsy-AfriSLM both narrows the AI gap for African languages and demonstrates that careful data curation and quality estimation can be more important than sheer dataset size or model scale in low-resource settings.

title: Metrics That Write Themselves: Evolving an Evaluator from Its Own Blind Spots
summary: Agents improve quickly against a reliable automatic metric and stall without one, and the applications that need them most, report generation among them, are the ones nobody knows how to score. Can the metric write itself? Saying what makes an answer good is hard; pointing at something wrong with one is easier, so the metric we evolve is a pool of small Python operators that each flag a candidate for one named defect, or abstain, and vote. Asking a model for operators directly does not work: 183 candidates realise only 96 distinct behaviours, from one narrow region of an enormous space. EvalCEGAR instead borrows counterexample-guided abstraction refinement from program verification. It reads the pool as an abstraction and searches for a collision, two answers the operators score identically, one correct and one not. That pair, not a prompt, is the authoring request, and when a collision defeats every attempt the loop widens what an operator may read rather than resampling. On MBPP+ and HumanEval+, a sandbox whose hidden unit tests give exact ground truth, the loop writes a 55-line operator that closes 15.4% of the gap between flagging nothing and a perfect filter on 428 unseen tasks (+0.0065, p=0.0010) at a quarter of our best hand-written operator's flags. On the benchmark it never saw it matches that operator's effect exactly on a third of the flags. Six of eight runs admit such an operator and all six help out of sample; our 15 hand-written operators applied together as one filter lose accuracy. An LLM judge on the same information ties that delta on a nearly disjoint set of candidates, and charges a model call per candidate forever where the operator charges none.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EvalCEGAR, a method that automatically learns code-based evaluation operators to judge model-generated answers by iteratively finding and fixing scoring collisions between correct and incorrect solutions, achieving significant gains on programming benchmarks without recurring inference cost.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents improve quickly when trained against reliable automatic metrics, but many important applications like report generation lack such metrics because defining what makes an answer good is hard. Manually written metrics or LLM judges are expensive, brittle, or require human expertise. The authors want a way for evaluation metrics to "write themselves" by exploiting the fact that it is easier to identify defects in bad answers than to specify all properties of good ones.
AI.method: They represent an evaluation metric as a pool of small Python operators, each designed to detect a specific named defect in a candidate answer, or abstain. Instead of directly asking an LLM to generate such operators—which leads to low behavioral diversity—they adapt counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) from program verification. EvalCEGAR treats the current operator pool as an abstraction, searches for collisions where two answers (one correct, one incorrect) receive identical scores from all operators, and then uses that pair as the query for the LLM to synthesize a new operator that can distinguish them. When no such operator can be found with the current input features, the system expands what information operators can read and repeats the loop.
AI.result: On MBPP+ and HumanEval+ benchmarks, where hidden unit tests provide ground-truth correctness for code solutions, EvalCEGAR automatically synthesizes a compact (~55-line) operator that closes about 15.4% of the performance gap between a trivial metric (flagging nothing) and an ideal perfect filter, improving accuracy by +0.0065 with statistical significance (p=0.0010) on 428 unseen tasks. This learned operator fires on about one quarter as many candidates as the best hand-written operator, yet on a held-out benchmark it matches that operator’s impact exactly on roughly one third of its flags. In six out of eight runs the method discovers such helpful operators, and all six transfer positively to out-of-sample data. In contrast, combining 15 hand-crafted operators into a single filter actually reduces accuracy.
AI.conclusion: EvalCEGAR can automatically synthesize effective, code-based evaluation operators for program-generation tasks by iteratively resolving scoring collisions between correct and incorrect answers. The learned operators provide statistically significant improvements while being lightweight and free to apply at inference time, and they can match or complement the effect of hand-written operators and LLM judges. This suggests a promising path toward self-authored, scalable evaluation metrics for tasks where ground-truth tests exist, particularly when human-authored metrics are hard to design and LLM judges are too costly or unreliable.

title: X2Streaming-TTS: Causal Token-Level Text-to-Speech from Streaming Text with Speech-State Inheritance
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Equal contribution by Rime Wen and Zehan Liu. Corresponding author: Hao Wang. Code: https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/X2Streaming-TTS
summary: Streaming text-to-speech is essential for low-latency spoken dialogue systems, yet many systems wait for sentence-level text and are therefore only pseudo-streaming. True token-level synthesis must generate speech from uncertain prefixes while maintaining perceptual continuity over an unbounded stream with bounded context. We present X2Streaming-TTS, a causal TTS framework that consumes asynchronously arriving text tokens and emits speech without accessing future input. To handle uncertain prefixes, we introduce causal commitment, which keeps ambiguous expressions provisional through uncertainty-aware buffering and performs capacity-adaptive, punctuation-aware segmentation. To preserve acoustic continuity, we further introduce causal speech-state inheritance, which carries the complete Code2Wav state and selected historical Talker states across segment boundaries. Together with an attention prior constraint, it blocks access to future positions while retaining bounded acoustic context. Experiments show that X2Streaming-TTS outperforms existing pseudo-streaming models on most subjective and objective metrics. Further analysis shows that causal commitment stabilizes online segmentation and reduces failures caused by insufficient context, while speech-state inheritance improves boundary continuity without degrading naturalness or speaker identity. X2Streaming-TTS thus achieves strict token-level synthesis with quality comparable to the evaluated offline baselines, a median time to first audio token (TTFT) of 15.8 ms for a single request, and a median TTFT of 260.8 ms at 128 concurrent requests. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/X2Streaming-TTS .

AI.tldr: The paper proposes X2Streaming-TTS, a truly streaming, token-level text-to-speech system that works with uncertain, partial text and maintains high audio quality and continuity with very low latency, even under heavy concurrency.
AI.motivation: Most current so‑called streaming TTS systems are only pseudo-streaming: they wait for sentence- or phrase-level chunks, which introduces latency and prevents truly interactive spoken dialogue. Achieving real token-level streaming is difficult because the system must speak from partial, uncertain text while preserving natural prosody and continuity over long, potentially unbounded input with only bounded context. The authors aim to close this gap and provide a practical, high‑quality, low‑latency streaming TTS solution.
AI.method: They introduce X2Streaming-TTS, a fully causal TTS framework that operates on asynchronously arriving text tokens and never looks at future input. The key techniques are: (1) causal commitment, which keeps ambiguous prefixes provisional via uncertainty-aware buffering and capacity-adaptive, punctuation-aware segmentation, so the system delays hard decisions until enough evidence appears; (2) causal speech-state inheritance, which carries forward the full Code2Wav acoustic state and selected Talker states across segment boundaries so the model maintains prosodic and timbral continuity despite segmentation; and (3) an attention prior constraint that enforces causal attention and bounded acoustic context, explicitly blocking access to future positions. They evaluate this system against existing pseudo-streaming models using subjective and objective metrics and measure latency (TTFT) under different concurrency levels.
AI.result: X2Streaming-TTS outperforms prior pseudo-streaming TTS systems on most subjective (e.g., human listening tests) and objective quality/continuity metrics. Analyses show that causal commitment leads to more stable online segmentation and fewer failures from insufficient text context, while speech-state inheritance improves continuity at segment boundaries without hurting perceived naturalness or speaker identity. The system delivers strict token-level synthesis with audio quality comparable to offline baselines, achieving a median time to first audio token of 15.8 ms for a single request and 260.8 ms at 128 concurrent requests.
AI.conclusion: The proposed X2Streaming-TTS framework successfully achieves strictly causal, token-level streaming TTS that can operate on uncertain, incremental text while maintaining high audio quality and continuity. Its causal commitment and speech-state inheritance mechanisms effectively handle uncertainty and boundary artifacts, enabling a practical, low-latency solution suitable for large-scale, multi-user spoken dialogue systems, with performance comparable to offline TTS baselines and publicly released implementation.

title: Pairwise Logical Selection of Enthymeme Completions under Semantic-Link Uncertainty
summary: Arguments often omit premises or claims, forming enthymemes. We study pairwise logical selection between two candidates for the omitted component. Existing natural language methods can identify or generate candidates but often do not expose how the selected candidate completes the inference, while logic-based approaches usually assume that the required formulae and background knowledge are available. We extend a prior neuro-symbolic pipeline from missing-premise to missing-claim selection and replace binary entailment outcomes with logical-resistance scores. Top-Link uses weighted Partial MaxSAT under a single configuration of highest-confidence semantic links. We then introduce Possible-World Atom-Link Formalization (PWAL), which keeps translated formulae fixed and marginalizes logical resistance over alternative cross-formula semantic-link configurations. We evaluate PWAL on five tasks: ARCT and a CDED-derived task for missing-premise selection, iDebate- and AAE2-derived tasks for missing-claim selection, and alphaNLI for abductive hypothesis selection. Relative to Top-Link, PWAL raises strict accuracy by 2.95-30.86 percentage points and reduces tie rates by 4.57-58.00 percentage points on all five tasks. When ties receive half credit, accuracy still increases by 0.45-6.04 percentage points. PWAL also records the translated formulae, sampled link configurations, and resistance components for every comparison, providing a transparent trace of each score.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PWAL, a neuro-symbolic framework for selecting the best missing premise or claim in enthymematic arguments, and shows it improves both accuracy and decisiveness over a prior method across five benchmarks while providing transparent reasoning traces.
AI.motivation: Enthymemes—arguments with implicit premises or claims—are pervasive in natural language, but existing methods either (1) select or generate missing components without clearly exposing how they complete the inference, or (2) use logic-based approaches that assume idealized, fully specified formal representations and background knowledge. There is a need for a method that can (a) operate over realistic text, (b) choose between alternative candidate completions, and (c) make its inferential process transparent and inspectable. The authors aim to bridge the gap between data-driven NLP and symbolic logic by offering a principled, explainable way to score candidate completions of arguments.
AI.method: The authors extend a prior neuro-symbolic pipeline that mapped natural language arguments into logical formulae linked by semantic relations and used weighted Partial MaxSAT for inference. First, they generalize from missing-premise to missing-claim selection and replace binary entailment decisions with graded logical-resistance scores that measure how hard it is to make an inference consistent. They propose two variants: (1) Top-Link, which fixes a single highest-confidence configuration of semantic links between formulae and performs MaxSAT-based reasoning, and (2) PWAL (Possible-World Atom-Link Formalization), which keeps the logical translations fixed but marginalizes over multiple alternative configurations of semantic links, integrating their contributions into a resistance-based score. The pipeline outputs both final scores and intermediate artifacts (formulae, links, components of resistance). They evaluate these methods on five datasets covering missing-premise, missing-claim, and abductive hypothesis selection tasks.
AI.result: Across five tasks (ARCT and a CDED-derived dataset for missing-premise selection; iDebate- and AAE2-derived datasets for missing-claim selection; and alphaNLI for abductive hypothesis selection), PWAL consistently outperforms the Top-Link baseline. It increases strict accuracy by between 2.95 and 30.86 percentage points and lowers the rate of ties—cases where the system cannot distinguish between candidates—by 4.57 to 58.00 percentage points on all tasks. Even when ties are partially rewarded (half credit), PWAL still yields 0.45 to 6.04 percentage point gains in accuracy. The system also logs detailed reasoning traces, including the logical translations, sampled link configurations, and decomposed resistance contributions for each comparison instance.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that PWAL provides a more robust and informative approach to selecting missing premises or claims in enthymematic arguments than earlier neuro-symbolic methods. By marginalizing over alternative semantic-link configurations and using logical-resistance scores, it improves both predictive performance and decisiveness while preserving transparency about how each decision is made. This suggests that carefully designed neuro-symbolic frameworks can effectively bridge natural language argumentation and formal logical reasoning, yielding systems that are both accurate and explainable across multiple argument-completion and abductive reasoning tasks.

title: Learning What to Fail On: Failure-Mode Contextual Bandits for Adversarial Data Curation
summary: We introduce a failure-aware adversarial retrieval-augmented framework for improving robustness in natural language understanding. Rather than selecting synthetic examples with a fixed reward threshold, our method formulates adversarial data curation as a failure-mode contextual bandit problem. Candidate examples are generated with retrieval-augmented prompting, filtered by the current target model, automatically validated by an LLM judge ensemble, and clustered into recurring failure modes. A stochastic policy then selects which failure modes to sample for retraining, and is updated using validation-based reward that balances robustness gains, forgetting, and data cost. This makes the data curator itself the learning agent, enabling adaptive selection of the most useful model failures across training rounds. On standard benchmarks, our approach improves RoBERTa-base accuracy from 88.48% to 92.60% on SNLI, from 75.04% to 80.95% on ANLI, and from 54.67% to 71.99% on MultiNLI, while consistently outperforming prior adversarial augmentation methods. We further demonstrate transfer to FEVER fact verification, achieving up to 79.86\% FEVER score and 82.45\% accuracy with RoBERTa-large. Finally, we provide a theoretical interpretation showing that, under stated assumptions, failure-mode sampling can reduce shortcut-aligned gradient contributions while inducing bounded distributional drift. By combining retrieval, automated validation, contextual-bandit failure selection, and controlled adversarial retraining, our framework enables scalable robustness improvement without additional human annotation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a failure-aware adversarial retrieval-augmented framework that treats adversarial data curation as a contextual bandit over failure modes, automatically mining and selecting challenging examples for retraining to improve robustness of NLU models without extra human annotation.
AI.motivation: Standard adversarial data augmentation often relies on fixed thresholds or static heuristics to select synthetic examples, which can be inefficient, costly, and may not target the most informative failure modes. The authors aim to design an adaptive, automated mechanism that discovers, organizes, and prioritizes model failures in a principled way so as to improve robustness while controlling forgetting and data cost.
AI.method: The method formulates adversarial data curation as a failure-mode contextual bandit problem. Synthetic candidate examples are generated via retrieval-augmented prompting, filtered by the current target model for likely failures, and then automatically validated by an ensemble of LLM judges. Validated failures are clustered into recurring failure modes. A stochastic policy over these modes is learned: at each round it selects which modes to sample examples from for retraining, using a reward signal based on validation performance that trades off robustness gains, catastrophic forgetting, and the cost of additional data. This policy is updated iteratively as the model and failure distribution evolve.
AI.result: On multiple natural language understanding benchmarks, the framework yields substantial gains: RoBERTa-base improves from 88.48% to 92.60% on SNLI, 75.04% to 80.95% on ANLI, and 54.67% to 71.99% on MultiNLI, consistently surpassing previous adversarial augmentation techniques. The approach also transfers to FEVER fact verification with RoBERTa-large, reaching up to 79.86% FEVER score and 82.45% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: By treating the data curator as a learning agent that operates over clustered failure modes, the framework can adaptively mine, validate, and select the most useful adversarial examples for retraining. Theoretical analysis suggests that such failure-mode sampling can reduce shortcut-aligned gradient components while keeping distributional drift bounded. Overall, the approach offers a scalable way to improve model robustness using retrieval, automated validation, and contextual-bandit-based failure selection, eliminating the need for additional human annotation.

title: Verifiable abstention makes AI leak diagnosis accountable in water distribution networks
comment: 42 pages, 5 main figures, 1 main table, 2 extended data figures, 3 supplementary figures, 15 supplementary tables. Code and data availability described in the paper
summary: Utilities lose a substantial share of treated water to leakage, yet rarely trust artificial-intelligence localizers to dispatch crews: guessing everywhere cannot justify excavation. The gap is accountability, not accuracy: no method proves when it should not act. Here we recast leak localization as decision-making under verifiable abstention. A physics-grounded executor agent falsifies hypotheses (leak, demand, sensor, valve) against a digital twin; an independent supervisor agent, with a large-language-model (LLM) auditor, checks evidence against a code-verifiable contract, then certifies a dispatch, requests evidence or abstains. Under field-grade noise, a 32% forced baseline becomes 96% decision precision on acted events. On an independently generated benchmark it acts on only 4 of 33 leaks, all correct. A 194-event register of audited real leak locations with twin-simulated pressures and flows yields five excavation dispatches, three correct, and 44% survey recovery at full district precision. Accountable abstention offers a defensible route to autonomous water-infrastructure operation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a leak-localization framework for water utilities that focuses on knowing when NOT to dispatch crews, using verifiable abstention to make AI-driven leak decisions accountable.
AI.motivation: Water utilities lose a lot of treated water to leaks but hesitate to use AI-based localization systems because these systems cannot justify their decisions well enough for costly excavations—especially their decisions about when they should refrain from acting. The core problem is lack of accountable, auditable decision-making rather than raw detection accuracy.
AI.method: The authors reformulate leak localization as a decision-making problem with verifiable abstention. They design a two-agent system: (1) a physics-grounded executor agent that tests competing hypotheses (leak, abnormal demand, sensor fault, valve issue) against a hydraulic digital twin of the network; (2) an independent supervisor agent, supported by a large-language-model (LLM) auditor, that evaluates the executor’s evidence against a formally specified, code-verifiable decision contract. The supervisor can then certify a dispatch, ask for more evidence, or abstain from acting. The framework is evaluated under realistic (field-grade) noise, on a synthetic benchmark, and on a real-world register of leak events with simulated pressures and flows from the digital twin.
AI.result: Under realistic noise, a baseline that is forced to always act has 32% precision, whereas the proposed system achieves 96% precision on those events where it decides to act. On an independently generated benchmark with 33 leaks, the system chooses to act on only 4, all of which are correct (100% precision but low recall, by design). On a real-world dataset of 194 leak events, the method recommends 5 excavation dispatches, of which 3 are correct, and achieves 44% leak recovery when considering survey-level detection at full district spatial precision.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling and verifying the option to abstain from acting, the framework delivers highly precise, auditable decisions suitable for costly interventions such as excavations in water networks. The results suggest that accountable abstention can provide a defensible pathway toward autonomous or semi-autonomous operation of water infrastructure, increasing trust in AI systems by making both actions and inactions justifiable under a formal contract.

title: Aslema at NADI 2026: Augmentation through Fewshot for SLU
comment: LLMs, Native, Arabic LLMs, Augmentation, Multilingual, Multimodal, Language Diversity, Contextual Understanding, Minority Languages, Culturally Informed, Foundation Models, Large Language Models, Audio Models, Omni Models, Slot Filling
summary: We present Aslema, our system for NADI 2026 Shared Task 5, which consists of two subtasks: intent recognition and slot filling. We evaluate four omni LLMs in a zero-shot setting and compare them with fine-tuned models. Our results show that fine-tuning consistently outperforms zero-shot inference. We further explore synthetic data augmentation by using an LLM to generate culturally grounded Tunisian Derja utterances, followed by voice cloning to generate synthetic speech. Incorporating this synthetic data improves performance on both tasks. Our final submitted system, based on Qwen3-Omni-30B and trained with a mixture of original and synthetic data, achieves 86.8% intent accuracy and 34.7 WER on the devtest split. On the official test set it ranks 1st in slot filling (59.5 CoER) and 4th among 8 teams in intent recognition (66.1% accuracy). We release our experimental scripts and will soon share the synthetic dataset to support further research in this area.

AI.tldr: Aslema is a system for intent recognition and slot filling in Tunisian Derja speech; fine-tuned omni LLMs plus LLM-generated/call-cloned synthetic data significantly outperform zero-shot and achieve top shared-task results.
AI.motivation: There is a need for effective spoken language understanding (intent recognition and slot filling) for Tunisian Derja, a low-resource dialect with limited labeled data. Existing large omni LLMs can be run zero-shot, but their performance on such dialectal, culturally grounded speech is unclear, and collecting real annotated speech is costly. The authors aim to (1) benchmark omni LLMs in this setting, (2) test whether task-specific fine-tuning is worthwhile, and (3) determine whether synthetic text and speech can meaningfully improve performance.
AI.method: The authors build Aslema for the NADI 2026 Shared Task 5, targeting intent recognition and slot filling. They (1) evaluate four omni LLMs in pure zero-shot mode; (2) fine-tune models, including Qwen3-Omni-30B, on available labeled data; (3) generate additional culturally grounded Tunisian Derja utterances using an LLM, then apply voice cloning to produce synthetic speech; and (4) train models on mixtures of original and synthetic data. They then compare performance across settings on the shared task devtest and official test splits using standard metrics (intent accuracy, WER, CoER).
