We compare zero-shot decoding, English-only fine-tuning, German-only diagnostic fine-tuning, two-stage EN->EN+DE continuation, and direct EN+DE fine-tuning across Whisper model sizes. Fine-tuning substantially improves MedASR performance, but the best model depends on the adaptation setting: Whisper-Medium gives the lowest English WER (7.72%) and the lowest combined EN+DE WER under direct EN+DE training (26.30%); German-only Whisper-Large-v3 gives the lowest German WER (44.96%), but as a within-corpus diagnostic on 86 single-speaker training utterances rather than robust generalisation. Layer-wise analysis of the two-stage Whisper-Small trajectory shows that English medical fine-tuning produces the dominant encoder shift, whereas multilingual continuation largely preserves the adapted representation space. Domain and language information remain highly recoverable across layers, while linearly recoverable error-predictive cues weaken as WER improves.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how fine-tuning OpenAI’s Whisper models for multilingual medical automatic speech recognition (ASR) changes their internal representations, beyond just measuring word error rate (WER).
AI.motivation: Medical ASR has to cope with specialised clinical terminology, scarce annotated data, and multilingual scenarios, where standard ASR models may not transfer well. While large pretrained models like Whisper already generalise strongly, we don’t fully understand what happens inside these models—especially in different medical and multilingual fine-tuning setups—if we only look at WER. A deeper representation-level analysis can reveal how domain and language adaptation actually reshape the model and which training strategies are most effective.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune various sizes of Whisper (Small, Medium, Large-v3) on medical English (EN), medical German (DE), and mixed EN+DE data under multiple adaptation schemes: zero-shot (no fine-tuning), EN-only fine-tuning, DE-only ‘diagnostic’ fine-tuning on a tiny dataset, two-stage EN→EN+DE continuation, and direct EN+DE joint training. They evaluate ASR performance via WER and analyse how internal encoder representations change, layer by layer. They probe layers to see how well domain (medical vs general), language (EN vs DE), and error-predictive signals can be linearly recovered, tracking how these properties evolve with fine-tuning and across adaptation strategies.
AI.result: Fine-tuning significantly improves medical ASR performance relative to zero-shot Whisper. The best configuration depends on language and training scheme: Whisper-Medium achieves the lowest English WER (7.72%) and also the best combined EN+DE WER (26.30%) under direct joint EN+DE fine-tuning. For German alone, Whisper-Large-v3 trained on just 86 single-speaker utterances attains the lowest reported German WER (44.96%), but this is more of a within-corpus diagnostic result than strong out-of-domain generalisation. Representation analysis of Whisper-Small under a two-stage EN→EN+DE trajectory shows that most encoder change occurs during the initial English medical fine-tuning; subsequent multilingual continuation mainly preserves this adapted representation space. Across layers, domain and language labels remain highly linearly decodable, whereas linearly recoverable signals that correlate with ASR errors become weaker as WER decreases.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual medical adaptation of Whisper yields sizeable performance gains, but the optimal model and training setup vary by language and adaptation goal. English medical fine-tuning drives the main restructuring of internal representations, and adding German later largely retains this adapted space instead of fundamentally reshaping it. Even after adaptation, the encoder strongly encodes domain and language, while features that linearly predict recognition errors diminish as models become more accurate. Representation-level analysis thus complements WER, clarifying how different fine-tuning strategies sculpt multilingual medical ASR models and offering guidance for future MedASR adaptation designs.

title: Eureka: Task-Conditioned Meta-Agent Orchestration for Scientific Discovery
comment: 62 pages, 1 figure
summary: We present Eureka, a task-conditioned Meta-Agent architecture that compiles long-horizon tasks into dynamic obligation graphs with explicit acceptance semantics. During execution, Eureka forms Macro-Agents with specialized state, memory, operators, tools, verifiers, and local topology via receding-horizon planning, architecture promotion, and minimal-sufficient compilation. When bottlenecks recur, cost-benefit-gated evolution updates the local architecture under constraints. Theoretically, we establish results on regret, planning invalidation, amortization, subtree interfaces, serializability, and verification. Experimentally, Eureka completes 170/170 recursive tasks and generates 3,948 certificates with no false acceptances. Active context compresses median input from 9,490 to 4,005 tokens; incremental processing avoids 65.38% recomputation across 12,000 tasks; 16,000 concurrent executions serialize consistently. The same Meta-Agent instantiates a Theory-Discovery Agent and a Math/Conjecture Agent. The former yields structural results in quantum-process and spacetime theory. The latter identifies bottlenecks in Riemann Hypothesis research and advances a positivity certificate for Suzuki's localized Weil quadratic form to 0 < a <= 69/200 = 0.345, reaching ~99.55% of (log 2)/2. These results suggest that scientific-agent capability depends not only on the base model but on whether an architecture can be formed to match the task's cognitive structure.

AI.tldr: Eureka is a meta-agent architecture that decomposes long, complex tasks into dynamic obligation graphs and specialized macro-agents, achieving strong theoretical guarantees and empirical performance on scientific reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing language-model agents struggle with long-horizon, recursive scientific tasks because they lack explicit task structure, dynamic specialization, and principled mechanisms for reuse, verification, and evolution of their own architecture. The paper aims to build an agent framework that can mirror the cognitive structure of complex scientific work, going beyond raw model capability, and to show that such an architecture can tackle demanding domains like quantum-process theory and the Riemann Hypothesis.
AI.method: The authors introduce Eureka, a task-conditioned Meta-Agent. It compiles complex tasks into dynamic obligation graphs with explicit acceptance semantics. At run time it forms Macro-Agents—specialized sub-agents with tailored state, memory, operators, tools, verifiers, and local graph topology—using receding-horizon planning, architecture promotion, and minimal-sufficient compilation. When recurring bottlenecks are detected, a cost-benefit-gated evolution procedure updates the local architecture under constraints. They also develop a supporting theory concerning regret bounds, when plans become invalid, amortization of computation, interfaces between subtrees in the obligation graph, serializability of concurrent executions, and verification guarantees. They then instantiate the Meta-Agent as a Theory-Discovery Agent and as a Math/Conjecture Agent and evaluate them on large suites of tasks and scientific case studies.
AI.result: Eureka successfully solves all 170/170 recursive benchmark tasks and produces 3,948 verification certificates without any false acceptances. Its active context management compresses median input length from 9,490 to 4,005 tokens, and incremental processing eliminates 65.38% of recomputation across 12,000 tasks. It also supports 16,000 concurrent executions with consistent serialization. In scientific applications, a Theory-Discovery instantiation produces new structural results in quantum-process and spacetime theory, while a Math/Conjecture instantiation analyzes bottlenecks in research on the Riemann Hypothesis and extends positivity certificates for Suzuki's localized Weil quadratic form up to a = 69/200, achieving about 99.55% of the theoretical target (log 2)/2.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that high scientific-agent performance depends crucially on the surrounding agent architecture—its ability to represent task obligations, specialize sub-agents, manage context, and evolve its own structure—not just on the base language model. Eureka demonstrates that a task-conditioned Meta-Agent with dynamic obligation graphs and macro-agents can deliver strong theoretical guarantees, large efficiency gains, robust concurrent execution, and nontrivial contributions to open scientific problems.

title: Assessing Quality of Experience in Natural Language Generation of German Text
comment: Dataset available at https://github.com/DFKI-NLP/TextQ/
summary: The rapid advancement of Natural Language Generation (NLG) has made the reliable evaluation of generated text increasingly critical, as these systems, such as large language models (LLMs), are now widely deployed in real-world applications. However, traditional automatic metrics fail to capture the multifaceted nature of perceived quality. In this paper, we introduce TextQ-German, a novel dataset suite for human-centered evaluation of German NLG from a Quality of Experience (QoE) perspective, covering automatic text summarization and machine translation. Through crowdsourcing studies with German speakers, we collect human quality ratings and identify relevant perceptual quality dimensions for each task. We develop automatic QoE prediction models, including transformer-based, linguistic feature-based, and hybrid approaches. Hybrid models outperform pure transformer baselines in almost all experimental settings, while linguistic features alone can approach the performance of fine-tuned language models. The dataset is extended with LLM-generated outputs annotated with overall QoE scores. Final validation on held-out sets indicates generalization to unseen data. Our work contributes a publicly accessible resource for NLG evaluation and baselines for automatic QoE prediction, providing a foundation for developing NLG systems that better align with human quality perception.

AI.tldr: Introduces TextQ-German, a dataset suite and models for human-centered Quality of Experience (QoE) evaluation of German NLG outputs in summarization and translation.
AI.motivation: As NLG systems, especially LLMs, are increasingly used in real-world applications, existing automatic metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE) are inadequate because they do not reflect the multifaceted, human-perceived quality of generated text. There is a need for resources and models that evaluate NLG outputs from a human-centered Quality of Experience perspective, particularly for the German language.
AI.method: They construct TextQ-German, a dataset suite for German NLG evaluation focused on summarization and machine translation. Using crowdsourcing with German speakers, they collect human quality ratings and determine key perceptual quality dimensions for each task. They then build automatic QoE prediction models: (1) transformer-based models, (2) models based solely on linguistic features, and (3) hybrid models that combine transformers and linguistic features. They also extend the dataset with outputs from large language models that are annotated with overall QoE scores. Finally, they test generalization via validation on held-out data.
AI.result: Hybrid models that incorporate both transformer representations and linguistic features consistently outperform transformer-only baselines in nearly all experimental configurations. Models using only linguistic features achieve performance close to fine-tuned language models. The generated dataset, including LLM outputs with QoE annotations, supports training and evaluation of QoE predictors and shows good generalization on held-out test sets.
AI.conclusion: TextQ-German provides a publicly available benchmark and resource for evaluating German NLG from a Quality of Experience viewpoint, along with baseline models for automatic QoE prediction. The findings demonstrate that combining linguistic features with transformer-based representations yields stronger QoE predictors than using transformers alone, and that well-designed linguistic features are highly informative. This work lays the groundwork for building NLG systems that more closely match human judgments of quality.

title: What is Missing from AI Post-Training AI: An Empirical Analysis
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can now post-train an LLM end-to-end. They can write code, launch training, evaluate checkpoints, and improve downstream performance, raising the prospect of AI-for-AI. We argue that this picture conflates two distinct capabilities: execution-level capability, iterating within a selected training strategy; and strategy-level capability, revising the high-level judgment as experimental evidence accumulates. Analyzing a large corpus of publicly released post-training trajectories, we find that across different tasks, the agent's training strategy is locked in at the very beginning, and the entire remaining budget is spent on local adjustments within the selected strategy. We then examine three natural explanations--missing experience, missing guidance, and insufficient reasoning--with escalating interventions. Extensive experiments show that (1) an experience-driven scaffold improves execution across the board (+12.6 points on GSM8K and +40.8 on HumanEval) but leaves the strategy static; (2) human guidance effectively redirects the initial strategy, yet the agent falls back into local adjustment loops once training starts; and (3) additional inference compute pays off on easier tasks but yields almost no gain on the hardest one. In conclusion, what agents lack is neither experience, guidance, nor reasoning compute, but a mechanism for spontaneously reevaluating their strategy during execution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why current LLM-based training agents can execute pre-chosen training pipelines well but struggle to change their overall strategy mid-course. By analyzing many real training runs and running controlled experiments, the authors show that agents almost never revise their initial strategy; they only tweak parameters locally. Even when given more experience, human hints, or extra reasoning compute, agents still lack a mechanism to spontaneously reevaluate and switch strategies during training.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can automate complex ML workflows, including code-writing, training, and evaluation, suggesting a future where AI systems improve other AIs autonomously (AI-for-AI). However, practical observations show that such agents often get stuck in repetitive local changes instead of making higher-level strategic decisions (e.g., changing the whole training pipeline when results stagnate). The authors want to understand whether this limitation is due to insufficient experience, lack of guidance, or inadequate reasoning, and what fundamentally blocks these agents from behaving like competent ML researchers who dynamically adapt strategy as evidence accumulates.
AI.method: 1) Corpus analysis: The authors collect and analyze a large corpus of publicly released LLM post-training trajectories across different tasks. They segment these trajectories into initial strategy selection and subsequent iterations, then measure how often and how substantially the overarching training strategy changes over time. 2) Intervention experiments: They design three escalating interventions to test hypotheses about the cause of strategy rigidity: (a) Experience-driven scaffolds that encode best practices and lessons from prior runs; (b) Human guidance that explicitly suggests alternative strategies or corrections at the outset; (c) Extra inference compute (e.g., more or deeper reasoning steps) to see whether longer deliberation enables strategy revision. They run these interventions on benchmark tasks such as GSM8K and HumanEval, and compare both performance gains and qualitative changes in training behavior (strategy switching vs. local tweaks).
AI.result: From corpus analysis, they find that the agent almost always fixes its high-level training strategy in the very first step and then uses the remaining compute solely for local adjustments (hyperparameter tuning, small code tweaks) instead of considering alternative strategies. In experiments: (1) The experience-based scaffold significantly improves execution quality and downstream performance (e.g., +12.6 on GSM8K and +40.8 on HumanEval), but does not lead to mid-course strategy changes; (2) Human guidance can successfully shift the initial strategy choice, but once training begins, the agent again gets trapped in local adjustment loops and does not conduct global reevaluation; (3) Allocating more inference compute helps on easier tasks but has little to no effect on the most challenging scenario, indicating that more “thinking time” alone does not unlock strategic flexibility.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM training agents exhibit strong execution-level competence but weak strategy-level adaptability: they can refine a chosen training plan but almost never reconsider or replace it as new evidence comes in. Their limitations cannot be fully explained by missing experience, absent human guidance, or insufficient reasoning compute. Instead, these agents lack an architectural or algorithmic mechanism that encourages or enables spontaneous strategy reevaluation during execution. Progress toward robust AI-for-AI systems will likely require explicit designs that support ongoing hypothesis revision and strategic exploration, not just better prompts, more data, or larger inference budgets.

title: SMTrap: Cost-Effective DoS Attacks Against Large Reasoning Models via SMT Conflict Guidance
summary: Existing LRM-DoS methods rely heavily on model feedback to synthesize attack queries, requiring either repeated queries to the target model or training a dedicated attack model. These expensive operations severely weaken attack leverage. In this paper, we propose \emph{search amplification}, a novel, model-feedback-free LRM-DoS paradigm. It employs the conflict count derived from an Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solver as a low-cost external signal to guide the synthesis of inference-heavy Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) instances. Our key observation is that LRMs depend on trial-and-backtracking search when solving CSPs, where higher SMT conflict counts on a given CSP instance positively correlate with more extensive LRM backtracking search and substantially longer output trajectories. Building on this finding, we propose \textsc{SMTrap}, a lightweight, CPU-only framework. Guided by SMT conflict counts, \textsc{SMTrap} generates inference-heavy CSP queries without model queries, attack-model training, or GPU computation. Evaluations across seven frontier models demonstrate the state-of-the-art LRM-DoS capability of \textsc{SMTrap}, producing DoS effects multiple times stronger than existing baselines. To mitigate the threat of \textsc{SMTrap}, we demonstrate a tool-based mitigation that significantly cuts token usage.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SMTrap, a model-feedback-free method to launch denial-of-service attacks on large reasoning models by generating constraint satisfaction problems that force extremely long inference through SMT-based search amplification.
AI.motivation: Existing large reasoning model DoS attacks require repeated interaction with the target model or training a separate attacker model, making them costly and limiting their practicality. The authors seek a cheaper, more scalable way to systematically produce queries that cause very long inference without relying on model feedback or GPUs.
AI.method: They observe that large reasoning models use trial-and-backtracking search when solving CSPs, and that the SMT solver’s conflict count on a CSP instance correlates with the model’s backtracking depth and output length. They define a search amplification paradigm that uses an SMT solver as an external oracle: the solver’s conflict counts guide the synthesis of CSP instances that are hard for LRMs. They instantiate this in SMTrap, a lightweight CPU-only framework that iteratively generates and refines CSP queries using SMT conflict counts, without querying the target model or training attack models.
AI.result: Across seven state-of-the-art large reasoning models, SMTrap produces denial-of-service effects that are multiple times stronger (in terms of token usage / inference cost) than prior LRM-DoS methods. It achieves this without model feedback, training, or GPU resources, demonstrating both high attack strength and low attacker cost.
AI.conclusion: Search amplification via SMT conflict counts is an effective and efficient paradigm for generating inference-heavy CSP queries that induce strong DoS effects on large reasoning models. SMTrap, as a CPU-only, feedback-free instantiation, outperforms prior attacks and exposes a practical vulnerability. The authors also show that tool-based mitigations can significantly reduce the induced token usage, suggesting a path toward defense.

title: Robust Risk Under Evolving Uncertainty: A Wasserstein Counterpart of the Entropic Value-at-Risk
comment: Best Paper Award at the 2nd Workshop on Safe AI at UAI (SafeAI@UAI 2026, non-archival), Amsterdam
summary: An agent still learning its environment should be cautious while ignorant and bold once confident. The entropic value-at-risk captures this through a robust-optimization identity---a confidence level fixes the radius of a relative-entropy ball of alternative models---but that ball cannot reach catastrophes the nominal deems impossible, precisely what a safe agent must hedge. We instead use an optimal-transport ball and study the coherent risk measure it induces, the Wasserstein entropic value-at-risk. It has a variational dual mirroring the entropic formula (an inverse temperature becomes a transport price), occupies a definite place in the risk hierarchy, and provably accounts for the reachable catastrophes the entropic measure ignores; we verify both dualities numerically. Driving the transport radius by belief entropy then yields a closed-form robust dynamic-programming operator whose caution contracts as the belief sharpens, with a certified safety sandwich and a sharp safety switch.

AI.tldr: They propose a new risk measure, Wasserstein entropic value-at-risk, for decision-making under model uncertainty that can hedge against catastrophic events ignored by classical entropic value-at-risk, and they embed it into a dynamic programming framework where caution adapts as an agent’s beliefs become more confident.
AI.motivation: Standard entropic value-at-risk (EVaR) models robustness by considering alternative probabilistic models within a relative-entropy (KL-divergence) ball, whose size is set by a confidence level. However, this approach cannot capture rare or catastrophic events that the nominal model assigns zero probability to, yet a safety-conscious learning agent should protect against such possibilities. The authors want a principled way for a learning agent to adjust its level of caution over time while still hedging against catastrophic but initially unseen events.
AI.method: They replace the relative-entropy ambiguity set with an optimal-transport (Wasserstein) ball, defining a new coherent risk measure called Wasserstein entropic value-at-risk (W-EVaR). They derive a variational dual representation for W-EVaR that parallels the classic EVaR dual form, with an inverse-temperature parameter playing the role of a transport price. They position W-EVaR within the known hierarchy of risk measures, prove that it accounts for catastrophic outcomes that classical EVaR misses, and verify the primal–dual formulations numerically. They then link the transport radius to the agent’s belief entropy, which leads to a closed-form robust dynamic-programming operator whose effective risk aversion automatically decreases as the belief distribution concentrates.
AI.result: The authors show theoretically that W-EVaR is a coherent risk measure with a clear dual formulation, that it belongs at a specific point in the lattice/hierarchy of risk measures, and crucially that it can hedge against catastrophic states that entropic risk measures fail to consider due to zero nominal probability. Their numerical experiments verify the derived dual representations and illustrate that W-EVaR captures the effect of reachable catastrophes. They also derive a dynamic-programming operator driven by belief entropy, demonstrating analytically that the induced level of caution contracts as the agent becomes more certain, while maintaining provable safety bounds (“safety sandwich”) and exhibiting a sharp transition (“safety switch”) between cautious and bold behavior.
AI.conclusion: Wasserstein entropic value-at-risk provides a principled way to incorporate distributional robustness against unseen catastrophic events into decision-making, overcoming a key limitation of classical entropic risk measures based on KL-divergence balls. By tying the size of the Wasserstein ball to belief entropy, the authors obtain a tractable robust dynamic-programming operator whose caution level adapts automatically as learning progresses, with formal safety guarantees. This offers a structured foundation for designing learning agents that are initially conservative but become more aggressive as their environment model becomes more accurate.

title: Test-Time Scaling in the Wild: Why Exploitation, Not Exploration, Is the Bottleneck
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves language model outputs by spending additional inference compute - generating multiple candidates, searching over partial sequences, or iteratively refining drafts. These techniques yield large gains on mathematics and code, but have been developed and stress-tested almost exclusively on tasks where verification is straightforward. We conduct the first compute-normalised comparison of five TTS families across five open-ended generation benchmarks spanning medicine, law, finance, general chat, and creative writing - grounded in a unified framework that decomposes the effectiveness of each method's token budget into exploration and exploitation. The answer depends on which side of that decomposition you examine. Scaling exploration works: the best candidate in the pool improves steadily with compute across all settings. What breaks is exploitation - the step that converts a rich candidate pool into a final output. With state-of-the-art generators, reward models correlate at only $ρ_v \approx 0.12$ with true quality, rendering selection near-random regardless of budget. Tree search amplifies this failure through diversity collapse. Refinement helps on one of five benchmarks; its apparent gains elsewhere are confounded. Only synthesis across candidates (Fusion) consistently improves over single-sample baselines, yet still recovers only ~40% of available quality. The candidate pool is not the bottleneck - choosing from it is.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates different test-time scaling (TTS) methods for large language models on open-ended tasks and finds that while generating more candidate outputs reliably improves the best-possible answer, existing methods for choosing or refining a final answer from these candidates are surprisingly weak.
AI.motivation: Most TTS methods—like sampling many outputs, tree search, or iterative refinement—have shown strong gains in domains such as math and coding, where answers are easy to verify. However, real-world use often involves open-ended tasks (medicine, law, finance, chat, creative writing) where verifying quality is much harder. There was no systematic, compute-normalised comparison of TTS methods in these settings, nor a clear understanding of whether limits come from not exploring enough candidate outputs or from poorly exploiting the candidate pool.
AI.method: The authors define a unified framework that decomposes TTS performance into exploration (how good is the best candidate we can generate with a given token budget?) and exploitation (how well can we pick or construct a final answer from the candidate pool?). They then run a compute-controlled comparison of five families of TTS methods—sampling-based pools, reward-model selection, tree search, refinement, and candidate fusion—across five open-ended benchmarks covering medicine, law, finance, general chat, and creative writing. They measure the correlation between reward-model scores and true quality, examine how tree search affects diversity, test refinement loops, and evaluate fusion strategies that combine multiple candidates into a single output.
AI.result: Across all benchmarks, increasing compute for exploration reliably improves the quality of the best candidate in the pool, demonstrating that test-time compute does create better options. However, exploitation is weak: state-of-the-art reward models show very low correlation (ρ≈0.12) with true quality, so selection among candidates is effectively near-random even with large candidate pools. Tree search tends to exacerbate the problem by causing diversity collapse, concentrating on narrow regions of the search space without reliably improving quality. Refinement only clearly helps in one of the five benchmarks, with apparent gains in others largely explained by confounders. Fusion methods—synthesizing a final answer from multiple candidates—are the only family that consistently beats single-sample baselines, but they still recover only about 40% of the quality available in the candidate pool.
AI.conclusion: The primary limitation of current TTS methods on open-ended tasks is not generating sufficiently good candidates, but rather the inability to reliably select or synthesize the best answer from the candidate pool. Reward models and search-based exploitation strategies are currently too weak and can even harm diversity. While test-time scaling remains promising, unlocking its full benefits for open-ended generation will require much better exploitation mechanisms—especially more reliable quality estimators and stronger methods for aggregating information across candidates.

title: Tuning the Stochastic Machine: A Systems Engineer's Operating Model for Human-AI Engineering
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Experience report and operating model
summary: When an expert corrects an LLM assistant's error, the correction usually dies with the session, and the error class returns. I argue this is an operations problem, not a tooling problem: mechanisms for persisting corrections exist and are shipping, but the discipline for governing them -- versioning with provenance, recurrence monitoring, counter-metrics, retirement of stale rules -- does not. Writing as a systems engineer of thirty years, I map the LLM stack onto the machines my profession already operates (frozen silicon, firmware, loadable modules, persistent configuration, volatile memory), identify where the mapping fails (stochastic generation, configuration that binds only probabilistically, no general-purpose retirement (verification) stage by default), and derive from the failures a seven-principle operating discipline with an error loop at its core. Three cases from my own practice illustrate the mechanism, among them a control that silently became the exact harm it was built to prevent. I close with the measurement framework this view implies and the lab study required to test it.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the main obstacle to learning from LLM error corrections is not missing tools but missing operational discipline, and proposes a principled “error loop” framework for governing persistent corrections across the LLM stack.
AI.motivation: LLMs repeatedly make the same kinds of mistakes even after human experts correct them, because those corrections are usually lost after the session ends or are not systematically managed. The author, with long systems-engineering experience, wants to bring mature operational practices (like versioning, monitoring, and retirement of rules) to LLM operations so that corrections persist, remain trustworthy, and do not turn into new failure modes over time.
AI.method: Conceptual and engineering analysis: the author maps components of the LLM ecosystem onto traditional system elements (hardware, firmware, loadable modules, persistent config, volatile memory). They then examine where this analogy fails for LLMs (stochastic behavior, probabilistic binding of configuration, lack of built-in verification/retirement stages). From these gaps, they derive seven operating principles centered on an error-feedback loop, and illustrate them via three real-world case studies from their own LLM operations practice.
AI.result: The analysis produces a structured operating discipline for managing LLM corrections, emphasizing persistent, versioned interventions with provenance; continuous monitoring for recurrence and side effects; counter-metrics to catch harms introduced by controls; and explicit deprecation/retirement of stale rules. The case studies demonstrate how such discipline would have prevented or mitigated failures, including one where a safety control gradually evolved into the exact harm it was meant to prevent.
AI.conclusion: Sustained improvement in LLM behavior requires treating corrections as operational assets governed like any other critical production configuration, not as transient chat events. A seven-principle operating discipline with an explicit error loop, supported by appropriate measurement and monitoring, can turn individual expert corrections into durable, auditable, and safe system-level behavior changes. The author calls for lab studies and a measurement framework to empirically test and refine this operations-centric approach.

title: MedUAG: Unified Understanding and Generation for Medical Multimodal Models
summary: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are rapidly evolving into unified understanding and generation (UAG) frameworks. However, extending these unified paradigms to the medical domain is hindered by: the absence of comprehensive training and evaluation benchmarks, and the lack of broadly validated unified medical model. To address these gaps, we present a comprehensive foundation for medical UAG. First, we construct MedUAGCorpus, the largest unified medical understanding and generation dataset to date, comprising over 6 million instances across 14 imaging modalities. Second, we introduce MedUAGBench, a systematic benchmark that expands medical generation evaluation to 12 diverse tasks under standardized protocols. Finally, leveraging these resources, we develop MedUAG, an end-to-end trained unified medical model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MedUAG achieves strong performance across a wide array of understanding and generation tasks, establishing a competitive baseline and paving the way for next-generation medical multimodal systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a unified medical multimodal understanding-and-generation framework built on a large corpus, a comprehensive benchmark, and an end-to-end model, achieving strong performance across many tasks.
AI.motivation: Multimodal large language models are becoming unified understanding-and-generation systems, but in medicine this progress is blocked by the lack of large, unified training data, standardized evaluation benchmarks for both understanding and generation, and an established unified medical model. The authors aim to fill these gaps so medical AI can benefit from UAG advances.
AI.method: The authors build three core components: (1) MedUAGCorpus, a large-scale medical multimodal dataset with over 6 million instances covering 14 imaging modalities, designed for unified understanding and generation training; (2) MedUAGBench, a benchmark defining 12 diverse medical generation and related tasks with standardized evaluation protocols; and (3) MedUAG, an end-to-end unified multimodal model trained on MedUAGCorpus and evaluated systematically on MedUAGBench.
AI.result: Experiments show that MedUAG performs strongly across many medical understanding and generation tasks, indicating that their unified model is competitive with existing approaches and provides a solid performance baseline for future research.
AI.conclusion: By providing a large unified corpus, a broad benchmark, and a strong unified model, the work establishes a foundation for unified understanding-and-generation systems in the medical domain and opens the path toward more advanced medical multimodal models.

title: Grouping the Stochastic Machine: Precision, Not Capability, as the Frontier Metric for AI Systems
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Companion to "Tuning the Stochastic Machine", submitted concurrently
summary: Frontier language models are compared, marketed, and benchmarked on capability -- what their best or average output can achieve. I argue this measures the wrong axis. The models have saturated accuracy: their mean output lands on the target. What now separates one system from another in practice is precision: how tightly concentrated their outputs are around that target across repeated, identical requests. Borrowing the marksman's distinction, capability is where the average shot lands; reliability is the size of the group. I make three claims. First, precision, not capability, is the frontier differentiator between systems, and benchmark culture systematically fails to measure it, reporting central tendency rather than spread. Second, precision is measurable, cheaply and without circularity, by running a fixed suite of deterministically scored tasks many times at fixed temperature and computing the per-task consistency of outcomes -- no model-in-the-loop grader required. Third, the measurement is not merely descriptive but decision-guiding: it separates consistent failures (a tight group off-centre, correctable by the operating discipline of Paper 1 -- a sight adjustment) from scattered failures (a wide group, correctable only by changing the model or its sampling -- a rifle problem). I define a grouping metric, specify a harness, and show how tracking a human-AI pair's grouping over time yields the compounding signal that Paper 1's field study requires. A first real run, since replicated, illustrates both the method and its most important limit: one measured gap was closed completely by a single rule (0/5 -> 5/5), while a suite of tasks authored from the rules themselves found no value, because a frontier model already embodies explicit good practice -- establishing that a discipline's worth is found by measurement on real work, not constructed from its own rulebook.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current evaluations of frontier language models focus on average capability, but the key differentiator now is precision/reliability across repeated runs; it proposes a simple metric and harness to measure this grouping and shows how it informs human-AI practice more than rule-based disciplines alone.
AI.motivation: Current LLM benchmarks emphasize capability (average performance) but frontier models already have high mean accuracy, so these metrics fail to distinguish systems or guide operational decisions. The author wants to shift attention to reliability/precision across repeated, identical prompts and demonstrate that this is both measurable and practically useful.
AI.method: The author borrows the marksmanship analogy (accuracy vs precision) and defines a grouping metric that captures how consistent a model's outputs are on deterministically scored tasks when sampled multiple times at a fixed temperature. They specify an evaluation harness that repeatedly runs a fixed task suite, scores each attempt without using another model as a grader, and computes per-task consistency to distinguish tight vs scattered error patterns. They then track a human-AI pair's grouping over time to see how reliability evolves in real work.
AI.result: A first real-world evaluation run (later replicated) shows that the grouping metric can isolate tasks with consistent, correctable failure modes versus those with inherently scattered performance. In one case a single operating rule turned a task from 0/5 to 5/5, showing how measurement can directly guide process fixes. However, when tasks are constructed directly from an explicit rulebook of “good practice,” the frontier model already performs well, revealing limited marginal value of such codified disciplines as opposed to measurement on real work.
AI.conclusion: Precision/reliability, not just capability/accuracy, is now the key axis on which frontier language models differ in practice. This dimension is currently under-measured because benchmark culture focuses on central tendency metrics. A simple, repeatable grouping metric and task harness can cheaply quantify reliability without circular grading, distinguish fixable process issues from model/sampling limitations, and generate the longitudinal signal needed for field studies of human-AI collaboration. Disciplines and rulebooks for using LLMs should be validated against measured performance on real work rather than against tasks derived from their own rules.

title: Institutional Newspapers Pipeline: Deriving billions of high quality tokens from historical newspapers
summary: Historical newspapers are an abundant record of public life, but their dense, irregular and sometimes noisy layouts make computational access to these materials both challenging and limited. We present the Institutional Newspapers Pipeline, a modular system we jointly designed with Boston Public Library to extract high-quality, structured datasets from historical newspaper scans. It was architected so that each step remains interpretable and customizable, and so that the pipeline as a whole remains computationally frugal enough to run on workstation-level hardware. The pipeline runs each scan through a multi-step process: it segments scans into individual type-agnostic crops and performs OCR on each resulting segment before then performing text analysis, type classification, reading order detection, named entities recognition, subject classification, language detection, and pre-computed embeddings generation on every crop. We ran this pipeline against a portion of Boston Public Library's holdings and released the results as an open dataset. The optical character recognition (OCR) output represents 16.3 billion o200k_base tokens across 83.1 million individual crops, extracted from 1,473,635 public domain newspaper scans published between 1795 and 1930. This report describes our methods for each processing step, the small models we trained, as well as the evaluation results and dataset-scale measurements we collected in the process. It accompanies the release of the pipeline, models, and dataset. We position this work as a substantial step towards unlocking high-quality data from tens of millions of newspaper scans.

AI.tldr: A modular, efficient pipeline to convert noisy historical newspaper scans into a large, structured, open dataset with OCR text and rich annotations.
AI.motivation: Historical newspapers contain valuable records of public life, but their complex, irregular, and noisy page layouts make them hard to process computationally at scale. Existing methods often lack interpretability, flexibility, or are too resource-intensive, limiting access for libraries and researchers who want high-quality structured data from large digitized collections.
AI.method: They designed the Institutional Newspapers Pipeline, a modular and interpretable multi-step system that runs on workstation-level hardware. For each scan, it segments the page into type-agnostic crops, runs OCR per segment, then applies multiple NLP and computer vision steps: text analysis, type classification, reading order detection, named entity recognition, subject classification, language detection, and generation of text embeddings. They trained small, task-specific models for these stages and evaluated each step, reporting both model performance and dataset-scale statistics.
AI.result: The pipeline was run on a large subset of the Boston Public Library’s historical newspaper holdings. It produced OCR for 16.3 billion tokens over 83.1 million crops, derived from 1,473,635 public-domain scans spanning 1795–1930. The outputs, along with the pipeline code and trained models, are released as an open dataset and tools. Evaluation metrics and large-scale measurements for each processing stage are documented in the report.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that their pipeline is a significant step toward making tens of millions of historical newspaper scans computationally accessible as high-quality structured data. By being modular, interpretable, and computationally efficient, it offers a practical, extensible foundation for libraries and researchers to unlock value from large digitized newspaper collections.

title: Beyond the Transcript: Detecting Covert Co ordination in Latent Multi-Agent Communication
summary: Language-model agents can communicate through continuous hidden states that are invisible in public transcripts, creating opportunities for covert harmful coordination. We introduce Verifiable Latent Alignments (VLA), an activation-aware framework for monitoring and steering these private communication channels. For every monitored decision, VLA links the private latent-state record and channel status to the resulting public action using a shared event identifier, enabling matched causal analysis. Our first contribution is a neutral-only three-layer monitor combining representation anomaly detection, counterfactual action-distribution influence, and sparse-autoencoder interpretation support. Our second contribution is a steerability framework spanning black-box behavioral instructions and white-box matched-neutral counterfactuals. Our third contribution is an evaluation on a controlled multi-agent auction benchmark covering homogeneous and heterogeneous model pairs, many-agent scalability, and intervention effectiveness. The sequential monitor achieves mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.993 for homogeneous agents and 0.854 for heterogeneous pairs when text- and latent-collusion rows are pooled as positives. In Qwen3-0.6B auctions with 25-100 bidders, monitoring requires only a small normalized load relative to all possible directed pairs, while full white-box steering achieves 100% bid-distribution recovery and reduces collusive low-bid behavior by 47.3 percentage points. Because full white-box steering replays the matched neutral counterfactual, its exact recovery is a sanity check by construction. Overall, the controlled study shows that the evaluated private channel attacks can be monitored without training the primary monitor on attack examples and mitigated when matched counterfactual access is available.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Verifiable Latent Alignments (VLA), a framework to detect and steer covert coordination between language-model agents via hidden-state communication channels.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents can coordinate through hidden activations that do not appear in text logs, enabling covert and potentially harmful collusion that existing text-only monitoring misses. The authors aim to make these private channels observable, analyzable, and steerable without needing attack-specific training data.
AI.method: They introduce VLA, which links each decision’s latent states and channel status to the resulting action via shared event IDs. The monitoring stack has three layers: (1) representation anomaly detection on activations, (2) counterfactual analysis of how channel use shifts action distributions, and (3) sparse-autoencoder-based interpretation for human-understandable features. For steering, they propose black-box behavioral instructions plus a white-box approach that constructs and replays matched neutral counterfactual trajectories to override collusive behavior. They evaluate on a controlled multi-agent auction benchmark under various agent configurations and scales.
AI.result: The sequential monitor attains very high detection performance (AUROC 0.993 for homogeneous and 0.854 for heterogeneous agent pairs when treating both text- and latent-collusion as positives). In auctions with 25–100 Qwen3-0.6B bidders, monitoring imposes only a small normalized load relative to all possible directed pairs. White-box steering using matched neutral counterfactuals fully recovers the non-collusive bid distribution and cuts collusive low-bid behavior by 47.3 percentage points, with perfect recovery guaranteed by construction when the counterfactual is replayed exactly.
AI.conclusion: Private communication channels via model activations can be effectively monitored and controlled by jointly leveraging anomaly detection, causal counterfactuals, and interpretable latent features, even without training the monitor on specific attacks. When matched neutral counterfactual access is available, white-box steering can reliably mitigate collusion, suggesting a viable path toward enforcing alignment over latent interactions between language-model agents.

title: DeepWeaver: Bridging the Evidence Synthesis Gap in Open-Ended Question Answering
comment: 49 pages, 6 figures
summary: Retrieve-then-generate pipelines are commonly used to produce deep-research answers for open-ended questions, but retrieval alone is insufficient: LLMs must organize noisy and fragmented evidence into comprehensive, well-cited answers. We refer to this process as evidence synthesis. However, direct generation often underuses evidence, misaligns citations, and collapses diverse information into shallow summaries, exposing an evidence synthesis gap between retrieval and generation. Thus, we propose DeepWeaver, a novel framework that weaves noisy retrieved evidence into comprehensive answers by maintaining Thought Block Chains (TBCs), a structured representation that groups claims, salient information, keywords, and supporting evidence. DeepWeaver uses subordinate TBCs to inspect residual evidence, commit TBC revisions, and discover new claims before final generation. We evaluate DeepWeaver on open-ended QA over both knowledge bases and the web, and introduce LoQA, a high-density benchmark for evidence synthesis. Across multiple LLMs, DeepWeaver improves content sufficiency, citation grounding, and detail preservation on LoQA, while achieving deeper insights and higher citation quality on DeepResearch Bench. These results show that evidence weaving is an effective mechanism for bridging retrieval and generation in open-ended QA. Our code is available at https://github.com/KlozeWang/DeepWeaver.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DeepWeaver, a framework that structures and refines retrieved evidence into better-cited, more comprehensive long-form QA answers using Thought Block Chains (TBCs), showing improved evidence use and citation quality on new benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieve-then-generate systems rely on LLMs to directly turn noisy, fragmented retrieved evidence into long-form answers. In practice, models often underuse evidence, misalign citations, oversummarize, and fail to preserve diverse details, leaving a gap between retrieval and final generation known as the evidence synthesis gap. The authors are motivated to design a mechanism that explicitly structures and iteratively refines retrieved evidence so answers are more complete, grounded, and insightful.
AI.method: The authors introduce DeepWeaver, a framework that maintains a structured representation called Thought Block Chains (TBCs). Each TBC groups claims, salient information, keywords, and their supporting evidence. DeepWeaver first constructs TBCs from retrieved documents, then uses subordinate TBCs to inspect leftover evidence, propose and commit revisions, and discover new or refined claims before producing the final answer. This process is applied with different LLM backbones on open-ended QA over knowledge bases and web data.
AI.result: On the newly introduced LoQA benchmark, which focuses on high-density evidence synthesis, DeepWeaver improves content sufficiency, faithfulness of citation grounding, and preservation of fine-grained details compared to standard direct generation pipelines. On DeepResearch Bench, a separate benchmark for deep research questions, the framework yields answers with deeper insights and higher citation quality across multiple LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Evidence weaving via Thought Block Chains is an effective way to bridge the gap between retrieval and generation in open-ended QA. By explicitly organizing and iteratively refining noisy retrieved evidence before final answer generation, DeepWeaver produces more comprehensive, better-grounded, and better-cited long-form responses. The authors release code to facilitate further research on structured evidence synthesis for LLM-based QA.

title: Structure, Association, and Decision Value: Representation-Based Difficulty Estimation for Adaptive Inference in African-Language NLI
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures, 10 tables. Submitted to MIRG-ICAIR 2026
summary: We ask whether internal representation statistics can provide useful example-level difficulty signals for adaptive inference in multilingual African NLP, and find that they cannot in this setting. Studying natural language inference across 15 African languages with frozen off-the-shelf checkpoints, we report four results. First, AfriXNLI's English configuration shares 1,047 of its 1,050 examples verbatim with XNLI evaluation data, and one widely used NLI checkpoint scores 1.000 on that test split, consistent with XNLI test exposure. Because AfriXNLI is derived from XNLI, its English, French and Swahili configurations cannot serve as clean evaluations for XNLI-trained models. Second, parameter count does not reliably order capability across African languages: our larger checkpoint is better in seven languages and worse in eight, with no significant aggregate difference. Third, across three multilingual representation spaces, angular dispersion is consistently more language-determined than effective rank, so pooled correlations can inflate one and mask the other. Fourth, the association that survives language control depends on the target: effective rank predicts probability gain from escalation but not whether escalation changes the prediction, while cheap-model confidence shows the opposite pattern; the two targets correlate at only 0.655. Under the tested models, signals, and compute budgets, no evaluated signal makes adaptive routing preferable to always-expensive inference, although an oracle exceeds it by 11 accuracy points at 60% of the compute. Our central methodological finding is that a representation statistic can be statistically significant for one notion of computational benefit while being irrelevant to another, and therefore be a poor decision variable.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether internal representation statistics can guide adaptive computation for multilingual African NLI and finds that, under tested conditions, they do not provide practically useful example-level difficulty signals.
AI.motivation: Adaptive inference aims to save compute by using cheap models on easy examples and expensive models on hard ones, but it requires good example-level difficulty signals. For African languages, resources and compute are often constrained, so such signals could be especially valuable. The authors want to know whether simple statistics of model representations (like effective rank and angular dispersion) can serve as these signals in multilingual African NLI, and whether existing benchmarks and assumptions about model size and performance are reliable in this context.
AI.method: They use frozen off-the-shelf multilingual NLI checkpoints and evaluate them on AfriXNLI across 15 African languages. They analyze (1) overlap and leakage between AfriXNLI and XNLI; (2) performance differences between larger and smaller checkpoints to test whether parameter count orders capability; (3) representation statistics (effective rank, angular dispersion) across three multilingual representation spaces; and (4) correlations between these statistics, model confidence, and different operational notions of computational benefit in an adaptive routing setting (e.g., predicting probability gain from escalating to a larger model vs. predicting whether escalation changes the prediction). They compare practical adaptive-routing policies to an oracle under fixed compute budgets.
AI.result: They find (1) AfriXNLI English shares 1,047/1,050 examples verbatim with XNLI test, and a common NLI checkpoint achieves perfect accuracy on that split, implying test exposure and making English/French/Swahili configurations unsuitable as clean evaluations for XNLI-trained models; (2) larger model size does not consistently improve performance across African languages— the larger checkpoint is better in seven languages and worse in eight, with no significant overall advantage; (3) across representation spaces, angular dispersion is more strongly driven by language identity than effective rank, so pooled correlations can misrepresent their behavior; and (4) after controlling for language, effective rank predicts probability gain from escalation but not whether escalation flips the prediction, while cheap-model confidence predicts flips but not probability gain, and these two targets themselves correlate only moderately (0.655). None of the evaluated statistics produces an adaptive routing policy that outperforms always using the expensive model under the tested compute budgets, though an oracle policy could beat it by 11 accuracy points at 60% compute.
AI.conclusion: Internal representation statistics studied here are not reliable decision variables for adaptive inference in multilingual African NLI under the tested models and budgets. Statistical significance of a representation measure with respect to one definition of computational benefit does not guarantee its practical utility for another, meaning that such statistics can be misleading if used directly for routing decisions. Benchmark contamination in AfriXNLI (via XNLI overlap) and the weak link between parameter count and performance further complicate evaluation and model selection in this setting.

title: Introducing the Privacy-HSD Trade-off: Hate Speech Detection, but not at the Cost of Privacy
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Accepted to WOAH 2026
summary: Hate speech is a real and timely threat that affects a large portion of online users, especially youth and minority groups. While building reliable and robust automatic hate speech detection (HSD) systems is paramount, we argue that this must also be balanced with the individual right to privacy. Exploring the intersection of HSD and privacy, we demonstrate that HSD systems might unintentionally achieve performance at the cost of encoding authorship, posing a threat to privacy. Building on these findings, we establish the notion of a privacy-HSD trade-off, which demands a careful balance. We benchmark a series of text privatization methods, as well as our newly proposed domain-specific AgnoSpeech technique, showing that balancing privacy and HSD is difficult but feasible. The findings make a strong case for more research on the trade-offs between privacy and HSD, both of which have tangible implications for the safeguarding of online participation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the trade-off between effective hate speech detection (HSD) and user privacy, showing that current HSD models may leak authorship information and proposing and benchmarking text privatization methods, including a new domain-specific method called AgnoSpeech.
AI.motivation: Online hate speech harms many users, but automatic hate speech detection systems, while necessary, may compromise user privacy by implicitly encoding information about who wrote a message. The authors want to understand and mitigate this privacy risk while preserving HSD performance.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze existing hate speech detection systems to see whether they encode authorship information, thus risking privacy leakage. They then formalize the idea of a privacy–HSD trade-off and evaluate multiple text privatization techniques designed to reduce identifiable authorship signals while keeping messages still usable for hate speech detection. They also propose a new domain-specific privatization method, AgnoSpeech, and benchmark it against other approaches.
AI.result: The study finds that hate speech detection models can indeed encode authorship, creating privacy risks. Their experiments show that there is a measurable trade-off between preserving privacy (e.g., obscuring authorship) and maintaining HSD performance. Among the evaluated methods, including their proposed AgnoSpeech technique, some can improve privacy while keeping hate speech detection accuracy reasonably high, though the balance is challenging.
AI.conclusion: There is an inherent privacy–HSD trade-off: making hate speech detection systems more accurate can inadvertently increase privacy risks by encoding authorship, but carefully designed privatization methods can partially mitigate this. The work highlights the need for continued research on methods that jointly consider user privacy and effective hate speech detection to support safer and more privacy-respecting online participation.

title: Grading the Graders: Verification Autonomy Levels (L0-L5) for LLM Reasoning
comment: Code and data: https://github.com/1549080929-debug/math_agent Keywords: LLM verification; verification autonomy; completeness; ground truth; trustworthy AI Writing and implementation assisted by an AI language model; all experiments, data, and research decisions are the author's own
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly paired with verifiers (step checkers, self-consistency filters, tool-based fact checkers, formal proof assistants) that claim to detect the model's errors. Yet the verification literature uses the word "level" to mean at least five different things: verification granularity, concept abstraction, risk tier, system-stack layer, and the epistemic source of the ground truth. We propose Verification Autonomy Levels (VAL), a meta-standard classifying verification schemes along a single axis: where does the verification spec come from, and what does the verdict guarantee? VAL ranges from L0 (LLM self-declaration, no deterministic anchor) through L2 (objective ground truth, correctness only) to L3/L4 (decidable systems with single-property or domain-level completeness), with L5 impossible in the unrestricted case. Central to VAL is the completeness blind spot: substitution- and sampling-based verifiers can confirm that proposed candidates hold, but cannot prove that no candidate was missed. We further identify a dichotomy the literature has not stated: completeness is reachable only for formally specifiable properties, while empirical open-world verification (fact-checking, diagnosis) caps at anchored correctness (L2). We document this across four domains (symbolic mathematics, behavior monitoring, medical diagnosis, and code generation) and in the strongest existing formal-verification baseline, whose authors note the verifier "focuses on the correctness of each step." We show the levels of granularity, concept hierarchy, risk, and system stack are orthogonal to VAL, resolving a systematic conflation across 17 surveyed papers. Code and full assessment are released as supplementary material.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified framework, Verification Autonomy Levels (VAL), to classify how LLM outputs are verified, focusing on where verification specifications come from and what guarantees they provide, and shows that true completeness is only achievable in formally specifiable domains.
AI.motivation: Existing work on verifying LLM outputs uses the term “level” inconsistently and conflates several orthogonal dimensions: granularity of checking, abstraction of concepts, risk categories, system architecture layers, and sources of ground truth. This makes it hard to compare methods and understand what reliability guarantees they truly offer. There is also confusion about what kinds of verification can ever guarantee completeness, especially for open‑world tasks like fact‑checking or diagnosis. The paper aims to clarify this conceptual landscape and set principled limits on what different verification approaches can guarantee.
AI.method: The authors introduce Verification Autonomy Levels (VAL), a single-axis taxonomy that classifies verification schemes primarily by (1) where the verification specification or ground truth comes from and (2) what kind of verdict guarantee is achievable. They define levels from L0 (pure LLM self-judgment) up to L4 (complete verification for a domain under a decidable formal system), and argue that L5 is impossible in unrestricted settings. They analyze the “completeness blind spot” of substitution- and sampling-based verifiers, then apply the VAL framework to four representative domains: symbolic mathematics, behavioral monitoring, medical diagnosis, and code generation. They also re-examine a strong formal-verification baseline to show how it fits into VAL and why it only guarantees step-level correctness. Finally, they survey 17 papers to demonstrate how dimensions like granularity, abstraction, risk, and system-stack layer are orthogonal to VAL and have been systematically conflated in prior work.
AI.result: The VAL framework distinguishes verification schemes by their epistemic grounding and the strength of their guarantees: from unverifiable self-assessment (L0), to anchored correctness against objective ground truth without completeness (L2), up to complete verification for formally specified, decidable properties (L3/L4). The analysis shows that existing verifier-augmented LLM systems mostly operate at or below L2 for empirical, open-world tasks, despite sometimes being described in stronger terms. The authors identify and formalize the “completeness blind spot,” showing that current substitution- and sampling-based techniques cannot ensure that better or alternative correct solutions were not missed. Their survey of 17 papers demonstrates pervasive conflation between VAL and other axes (granularity, abstraction, risk tier, system layer), clarifying that these are orthogonal properties of verification setups.
AI.conclusion: Verification Autonomy Levels (VAL) provides a principled, single-axis standard to classify LLM verification schemes by their source of specification and guarantee strength, separating this from orthogonal dimensions like granularity, risk, and abstraction. The work argues that completeness is only attainable in domains with formally specifiable, decidable properties and that open-world verification tasks are fundamentally limited to correctness relative to an external ground truth (L2), not completeness. This clarifies what current verifier-augmented LLMs can and cannot promise, highlights the inherent limitations of empirical verifiers, and offers a common vocabulary to more accurately describe, compare, and design verification methods for LLM systems.

title: Institutional Books - Enriched Text: A customizable multilingual open-source pipeline for denoising, deduplicating, and annotating OCR text at scale
summary:
Released in 2025, Institutional Books: Harvard Library (IB-HL) is a collection of 983,004 volumes (242B o200k_base tokens), originally digitized through Harvard Library's participation in the Google Books Library project. As researchers and developers have begun to use IB-HL, a tension has emerged between standard large-scale preprocessing practices and the goals of careful information stewardship. Many existing pipelines optimize for web text: as a result, they tend to aggressively filter, deduplicate, restrict by language, and sometimes discard meaningful metadata. Meanwhile, researchers seeking to use IB-HL duplicate effort while performing similar processing and analysis.
  We describe an approach that we call Enriched Text. Instead of producing a single 'complete' stream of tokens, we normalize the text while preserving metadata through annotations. We separate endmatter, detect per-paragraph language, identify clusters of duplicate paragraphs, and compute per-paragraph bits-per-byte scores. We provide this information through HTML-like annotations layered on top of the text. By parsing these annotations, users can tailor the output to their own needs instead of accepting a global editorial decision on content. The pipeline applies to all $\approx$250 languages in the collection.
  This report describes this project's goals, implementation, and design rationale. The release includes IB-HL-ET (an enriched-text version of IB-HL containing 217B o200k_base tokens across 983,003 volumes, organized into 1.39B annotated subtopic paragraphs) and the pipeline that produced it. These serve to make the collection easier for machines to parse and for humans to study.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Institutional Books: Harvard Library (IB-HL), a massive digitized book corpus, and presents an Enriched Text pipeline that preserves rich metadata via annotations instead of a single flattened token stream.
AI.motivation: Standard large-scale text preprocessing pipelines are optimized for web text and typically over-filter, deduplicate, enforce strict language restrictions, and discard valuable metadata. This clashes with goals of careful information stewardship and causes different researchers working on the same collection (IB-HL) to repeatedly implement similar processing steps independently. The authors want a way to support diverse research needs without imposing one global editorial decision on the text.
AI.method: They propose an Enriched Text approach that normalizes book text while preserving detailed metadata as HTML-like annotations layered on the text. The pipeline separates endmatter, detects language at the paragraph level, identifies clusters of duplicate paragraphs, and computes per-paragraph bits-per-byte scores. These annotations allow users to selectively include or exclude content and metadata depending on their application. The pipeline is designed to be applicable across approximately 250 languages contained in IB-HL.
AI.result: They release IB-HL-ET, an enriched-text version of the IB-HL corpus, containing 217B o200k_base tokens across 983,003 volumes, segmented into 1.39B annotated subtopic paragraphs. Alongside the corpus, they release the processing pipeline that generated it. The corpus is now more machine-parseable and analytically useful due to the structured annotations and standardized preprocessing.
AI.conclusion: Enriched Text offers a flexible alternative to monolithic preprocessing for large text corpora, enabling researchers to make context-dependent choices using preserved metadata rather than being constrained by a single global filtering and normalization pass. The IB-HL-ET release and its pipeline improve both machine and human access to the IB-HL collection by providing rich, structured annotations at scale.

title: Intercepting the Kangaroo: Experimental Astrolinguistics with Constructed Lexicons, Active Probing, and Large Language Models as Informants and Hypothesis Proposers
summary: Astrolinguistics -- communication with minds that categorize reality differently from ours -- has been purely speculative since Freudenthal's Lincos (1960). We make it experimental. Two language models with deliberately incompatible constructed lexicons (one encoding shape, color, and motion; the other fusing color with motion, encoding parity, and lacking shape) serve as informants with complete ground truth, while a fully scripted orchestrator translates between the two category systems. The central failure mode is the kangaroo effect: the silent attachment of a word to the wrong referent -- Quine's indeterminacy of translation, operationalized. Across 400+ simulated and live runs, a protocol combining cross-situational elimination, pre-registered predictive probes, active scene selection, a stricter recovery round, and quarantine produced no undetected mistranslations under the tested conditions and exceeded a passive baseline's coverage (d = 0.62). Injected kangaroo traps defeated naive ostension and pure statistical learning in 100% of runs, while the full protocol intercepted every decoy and, where discriminating evidence is ontologically unavailable, declared Quinean equivalence classes instead of guessing. Under informant noise it degrades gracefully: zero kangaroos persist up to 2% per-word noise; at 10% the protocol predominantly abstains rather than errs. Finally, words outside the scripted hypothesis space (a history-dependent relational term and an XOR contextual homonym) are recovered by a generate-and-test loop in which an LLM proposes rules and the script verifies them: coverage scales with proposer capability (0% -> 18% -> 72% -> 100%) while undetected mistranslations stayed at zero throughout. In the tested conditions, correctness is a property of the protocol; coverage is a property of the instruments.

AI.tldr: The paper turns astrolinguistics—communication with minds whose concepts differ radically from ours—from a philosophical idea into an experimental problem using language models with incompatible lexicons.
AI.motivation: Astrolinguistics has long been speculative, focusing on how to communicate with entities that carve up reality using fundamentally different conceptual categories (e.g., aliens, radically different AIs). Philosophers like Quine highlighted the indeterminacy of translation, where a word can be silently mapped to the wrong concept (“kangaroo effect”), but there has been little empirical work on practical translation protocols that can detect and avoid such failures.
AI.method: The authors construct two artificial languages with intentionally mismatched semantic categories: one encodes shape, color, and motion; the other fuses color with motion, encodes parity, and lacks shape. Two language models act as informants, each fluent in one lexicon and grounded in a shared simulated world. A fully scripted orchestrator mediates interaction, using a protocol that combines cross-situational elimination, pre-registered predictive probes, active selection of diagnostic scenes, a stricter recovery round, and a quarantine mechanism for suspicious hypotheses. They also inject designed “kangaroo traps” to test the protocol, introduce controlled informant noise, and add unscripted word types (history-dependent relational terms, XOR-contextual homonyms). For these out-of-hypothesis words they use a generate-and-test loop, where an LLM proposes candidate semantic rules and the script verifies them.
AI.result: Across over 400 simulated and live runs, the full protocol achieved zero undetected mistranslations (no surviving kangaroos) under tested conditions and outperformed a passive baseline in semantic coverage with a medium effect size (d = 0.62). Injected kangaroo traps completely fooled naive pointing-based learning and pure statistical methods, but were always caught by the full protocol, which sometimes output Quinean equivalence classes rather than a single guess when evidence could not distinguish meanings. Under noise, the protocol maintained zero mistranslations up to 2% per-word corruption; at 10% noise it mostly abstained instead of making errors. For words outside the initial hypothesis space, coverage improved monotonically with the power of the LLM proposer (from 0% to 100%), while the rate of undetected mistranslations remained at zero.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that, within the tested setup, translation correctness can be guaranteed by a sufficiently careful protocol, while how much can be learned (coverage) depends on the cognitive power of the informant and hypothesis generator. It operationalizes Quine’s indeterminacy of translation (“kangaroo effect”) and shows how an experimental, tool-augmented procedure can detect and avoid hidden mistranslations, offering a template for robust communication with agents that use fundamentally different conceptual schemes.

title: Comment-level Topic Drift Analysis in the Reddit Corpus
summary: We present a novel application of embedding-based dynamic topic modeling techniques to detect and quantify topic drift at the comment level in a massive corpus. By leveraging pretrained language models to generate contextualized semantic embeddings for short text, we analyzed 12.7 billion Reddit comments spanning 2006 to 2022. Using unsupervised methods on these embeddings, we identify dynamically evolving topic clusters over time. Our primary contribution is a methodology for analysis of semantic drift and discourse evolution in the embedding space itself. We also demonstrate modifications to existing methods that enable this analysis at scale, and we propose and demonstrate a null model comparison test to filter spurious dynamics. Key findings suggest that politically and socially contentious topics exhibit significant directional drift in embedding space, with inter-topic distances changing systematically over time beyond what the null model can explain, whereas domains such as music and sports remain comparatively stable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an embedding-based dynamic topic modeling framework to detect and quantify how discussion topics drift over time in a massive Reddit comment corpus.
AI.motivation: Traditional topic modeling struggles with short texts and with capturing fine-grained temporal evolution of topics, especially at very large scale. The authors aim to develop a method that can detect semantic drift and discourse evolution over time at the comment level, leveraging modern language model embeddings and handling billions of documents.
AI.method: They use pretrained language models to create contextual semantic embeddings for each Reddit comment (12.7 billion from 2006–2022). On these embeddings, they apply unsupervised clustering methods to discover topic clusters that evolve over time, effectively performing dynamic topic modeling in embedding space. They adapt and scale existing methods to work on this very large dataset and design a null model comparison test to distinguish genuine temporal dynamics in topics from spurious changes or noise.
AI.result: The method identifies dynamically evolving topic clusters and measures their trajectories and distances in embedding space over time. The null model helps filter out apparent topic shifts that can be explained by randomness or sampling effects. Empirically, they observe that topics related to politically and socially contentious issues show strong, systematic directional drift and changing inter-topic distances beyond what the null model predicts, while topics such as music and sports show relatively little drift and remain stable.
AI.conclusion: Embedding-based dynamic topic modeling at scale is feasible and provides a powerful way to quantify semantic drift in online discourse.
