The observed strong drift for contentious topics versus stability for entertainment domains suggests that this approach can reveal how public conversation around sensitive issues changes over time, and that embedding-space analysis combined with null models is effective for separating real discourse evolution from noise.

title: ChildSafeAds Shared Task 2026: Commercial Content in Child-Facing YouTube Videos
summary: ChildSafeAds is a shared task on commercial content in YouTube videos likely to reach children and teenagers. It contains 3,360 videos from 939 channels. Each instance begins with a segment submitted to SponsorBlock, an open-source crowdsourced browser extension whose users mark sponsor segments so that others can skip them. We pair the segment with its available transcript, video and channel information, and a sales or service page linked from the video description. Systems determine what kind of offer is being promoted (ST1), assign product categories (ST2), and identify legal risk flags (ST3). The evidence is divided into four cumulative access levels, from the transcript to the linked page, so results can be compared against the cost of collecting the data. 45.5\% of videos in our data failed to properly use the in-platform ad disclosure method (the ``Includes paid promotion'' label). GPT-5.4 produced the labels after the expert organiser team reviewed samples and iterated on the taxonomy, prompts and model choices. GPT-5.6-luna independently labelled the development set. This report describes the task, data and evaluation. An updated version will add participating systems and shared-task results.

AI.tldr: Introduces ChildSafeAds, a shared task and dataset for detecting and analyzing commercial content in YouTube videos likely viewed by minors, with multiple subtasks and graded evidence levels.
AI.motivation: There is growing concern about commercial content and advertising practices targeting or reaching children and teenagers on platforms like YouTube, including inadequate ad disclosures and potential legal risks. Researchers and regulators need structured data and benchmarks to study what is being promoted, how it is categorized, and whether it raises legal concerns. Existing resources do not provide a well-annotated, multi-modal benchmark focused on child-directed or child-accessible online video ads. The paper aims to fill this gap by introducing a shared task and dataset to support the development and evaluation of automatic systems that can detect and categorize such commercial content and its compliance issues.
AI.method: The authors construct the ChildSafeAds dataset from 3,360 YouTube videos across 939 channels, focusing on segments marked as sponsor content via SponsorBlock, a crowdsourced tool whose users label segments containing sponsor messages. For each instance, they compile multiple evidence sources: the sponsor segment itself, its available transcript, metadata about the video and channel, and a linked sales or service page. They define three subtasks: (ST1) classify the type of offer being promoted, (ST2) assign detailed product categories, and (ST3) identify legal risk flags. They organize evidence into four cumulative access levels, from using only the transcript up to including the linked external page, to compare performance versus data collection cost. Labels are generated using large language models (GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.6-luna) in an iterative, expert-guided process: experts refine the taxonomy, prompts, and model settings, then GPT-5.4 produces labels for the corpus, and GPT-5.6-luna independently labels the development set. The paper outlines the task, the dataset construction, and the evaluation setup, with a promise to later add results from participating systems.
AI.result: Key descriptive results include: (1) a curated multi-modal dataset of 3,360 sponsor segments from 939 YouTube channels, each enriched with transcripts, metadata, and linked commercial pages at varying access levels; (2) a taxonomy for offer types, product categories, and legal risk flags; (3) initial analysis showing that 45.5% of videos in the dataset did not properly use YouTube’s built-in ad disclosure label ("Includes paid promotion"), indicating widespread disclosure non-compliance in the sampled data; and (4) high-coverage automatic labeling produced by GPT-5.4, with an independently labeled development set from GPT-5.6-luna to support evaluation and research on model agreement and reliability. The main quantitative evaluation of systems is deferred to an updated version after shared-task participation.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes ChildSafeAds as a new shared task and benchmark for studying commercial content in YouTube videos likely to reach minors, with clearly defined subtasks on offer type, product categorization, and legal risk detection, and with a structured, multi-level evidence design. The dataset and task enable systematic research into automated detection and analysis of online advertising practices, especially around disclosure and legal compliance, and show that mislabeling or under-disclosure of sponsored content is common in the collected sample. Future work, to be reported in an updated version, will present the performance and methods of participating systems, enabling comparative evaluation and further advances in child-safe advertising analytics.

title: SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments
comment: Work in progress. Project page: https://spade-rl.github.io ; Code: https://github.com/spade-rl/spade
summary: Continuous self-improvement requires an ever-expanding pool of self-generated, diverse, adaptive goals. For language agents, existing training environment pools (hand-curated, statically synthesized, or frozen-verifier) keep the goal distribution fixed as the learner scales. We introduce SPADE (Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments), a self-play RL framework in which a single LLM plays two roles: an Environment Designer that writes complete, long-horizon training environments as executable code with an OpenAI Gym-style reset()/step() interface, and a Reasoning Agent that learns to act in them. Each is a stateful, multi-turn environment (state transitions, reward functions, and verification code), so one interface spans reasoning problems and multi-step agentic tool use. The Reasoning Agent's regret is estimated using the gap between its reward with and without privileged hints; in optimizing this regret signal the Environment Designer learns to target environments at the edge of the agent's capabilities while keeping them feasible. Through extensive experimentation, we find several components critical to success: grounding the Environment Designer on documents sampled from a large pretraining corpus, and giving it an accumulated environment memory. Scaling to 30B-parameter models, SPADE improves over the strongest fixed-environment baseline by +5.3 on average across eight held-out math, science, code, and reasoning benchmarks, and lifts the tool-use setting by +5.7 on BFCL-v4 multi-turn and +13.9 on ACEBench-Agent; on the games setting, the margin over the strongest baseline grows with model scale. By making environment design itself a learnable component, SPADE takes a concrete step toward open-ended self-improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SPADE, a self-play reinforcement learning framework where a single large language model acts both as an environment designer and a reasoning agent, generating adaptive executable training environments that drive open-ended self-improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing training setups for language agents rely on fixed sets of environments or tasks, which do not adapt as the model scales and thus limit continuous self-improvement and open-ended learning. The authors want a system where the task distribution can evolve and stay at the frontier of the agent’s capabilities without manual curation.
AI.method: SPADE uses a single LLM in two roles: (1) Environment Designer, which writes full training environments as executable code exposing a reset()/step() API (similar to OpenAI Gym), including state transitions, rewards, and verifiers; and (2) Reasoning Agent, which learns to act in these environments via self-play RL. The framework computes a regret signal by comparing the agent’s performance with and without privileged hints, and the Environment Designer is optimized to create environments that maximize this regret while remaining solvable. The designer is grounded using documents sampled from a large pretraining corpus and maintains an accumulated memory of past environments, enabling more diverse and sophisticated environment generation. Training is scaled up to 30B-parameter models and evaluated across multiple domains and benchmarks.
AI.result: SPADE-trained models outperform the strongest fixed-environment baselines by an average of +5.3 points across eight held-out benchmarks spanning math, science, code, and reasoning. In tool-use settings, SPADE yields gains of +5.7 on BFCL-v4 multi-turn and +13.9 on ACEBench-Agent. In game environments, performance margins over baselines grow as model size increases, indicating favorable scaling behavior.
AI.conclusion: By making environment design a learnable and adaptive component driven by self-play and regret-based feedback, SPADE enables language models to continuously generate challenging yet solvable training tasks, demonstrating concrete progress toward open-ended self-improvement for language agents.
